title: Jimi Hendrix’s final words to roadie revealed after violent Hells Angels clash
summary: Eric Barrett recalls Jimi Hendrix's final concert at the Isle of Fehmarn, where Hells Angels violence forced a harrowing escape before his death.
story: Carlos Santana recalls the moment he impressed Jimi Hendrix
It was supposed to be another stop on the road for Jimi Hendrix — but a festival marred by violence and chaos would become the rock legend's final official concert performance.

Eric Barrett, who was Hendrix's roadie and confidant from 1968 to 1970, has written a memoir, "Experienced: On the Road with Jimi Hendrix and Beyond." Barrett went on to spend nearly five decades working behind the scenes with other iconic artists, including Madonna, David Bowie and Aerosmith.

"We were playing on the Isle of Fehmarn, and the Hells Angels had taken over," Barrett recalled to Fox News Digital. "There was no control. It was a scary place to be. We had two cars there waiting to get us off the island and go back to London. But the Hells Angels didn't want us to get off the island. They wanted the boys to stay and party. And then it got violent."
PAUL MCCARTNEY REVEALS HOW A 'HAPPY' TEEN HITCHHIKING TRIP WITH GEORGE HARRISON DELIVERED A SHOCK
Jimi Hendrix is the subject of a new book by his roadie and tour manager, Eric Barrett, titled, "Experienced: On the Road with Jimi Hendrix and Beyond." (David Redfern/Redferns)

According to Barrett's book, hundreds of Hells Angels descended on the island and took over the venue. He wrote that many fans who had been camping out were "beaten and robbed" as festival security was chased off. Hendrix, he said, took one look at the mayhem and retreated to his room "alone, sober." The outlaw motorcycle club had taken over.

The next day, Hendrix took the stage and was met with boos. He told the hostile audience, "I don't give a f--- if you boo, as long as you boo in key, you mothers," before chuckling. When he was done, Hendrix told the audience, "Thank you, goodbye. Peace!"
"Experienced: On the Road with Jimi Hendrix and Beyond" by Eric Barrett is out now. (Diversion Books)
Barrett ushered Hendrix and the band off the stage toward the waiting cars. Barrett was eager to get out. But then the bikers surrounded them.
WATCH: CARLOS SANTANA RECALLS THE MOMENT HE IMPRESSED JIMI HENDRIX: ‘I’LL TAKE IT’

"I saw a Hells Angel about to hit [tour manager] Gerry Stickells over the head with this baton," said Barrett. "I put my arm up to take the blow. I nearly passed out from the pain, but imagine if it had landed on Gerry's skull? We managed to get inside the car. Jimi kept looking at me because he saw me take the blow. He just said to me, 'Are you OK, Eric? Are you OK?' He kept asking me if I was OK. That's just the kind of man he was. And... that was the last thing he ever said to me."
Eric Barrett was Jimi Hendrix's roadie from 1968 to 1970. (Courtesy of Eric Barrett)
On Sept. 18, 1970, paramedics arrived at Monika Dannemann's apartment at the Samarkand Hotel in London and found Hendrix unresponsive. He was 27.
Stickells broke the news to Barrett.
An exterior view of the former Samarkand Hotel in London, where Jimi Hendrix died in 1970. (Future Publishing via Getty Images)

"I couldn't believe it," said Barrett. "I remember walking around London in a fog. It was a stupid, tragic accident. He took too many of [girlfriend] Monika Dannemann's sleeping pills. She supposedly had these incredibly powerful German tranquilizers. And she said he took nine of them. She couldn't wake him. She called Eric Burdon of The Animals, who was a good friend of Jimi's. He screamed at her, 'Call the f-----g ambulance!'"
From left: Friends Jimi Hendrix, Eric Burdon and Noel Redding. (Sygma via Getty Images)
"What I'm being told was the ambulance guys ... laid him on his back, and he threw up," said Barrett. "He asphyxiated. That was the accident. The pills were the accident. Tragedy was him dying."
Jimi Hendrix performs at the Isle of Wight festival on August 29, 1970. (Jean-Pierre Leloir)

In the book, Barrett wrote, "The paramedics arrived but couldn't revive Jimi. They carried him out on a stretcher to the ambulance, assuring Monika that he was going to be all right. Either lying in bed on his back or on the way to the hospital, Jimi threw up on himself. The post-mortem concluded that Jimi had died of asphyxia while intoxicated with barbiturates."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Monika Dannemann is seen here outside the building where Jimi Hendrix died. (Brian Aris/Mirrorpix)

"... I flashed back to the time I took too much Mandrax, and my girlfriend couldn't wake me up," he wrote. "It was easily done and could've happened to any of us in Jimi's group of friends. That it happened to Jimi himself was heartbreaking. But I've never heard anything to make me think Jimi's death was anything other than what it appeared."
Rock guitarist Jimi Hendrix is seen here with Eric Barrett at Heathrow Airport after flying in from New York on his way to the Isle of Wight pop festival. (PA Images via Getty Images)

Barrett firmly rejected the rumors and conspiracy theories that have surrounded Hendrix's death for decades. Among them was an allegation by former roadie James "Tappy" Wright, who wrote in his 2009 memoir, "Rock Roadie," that Hendrix’s manager, Mike Jeffery, confessed to killing Hendrix, The Guardian reported.
Barrett strongly disputes Wright's account and rejects any suggestion that Hendrix was murdered.
Manager Michael "Mike" Jeffery is seen outside Marylebone Register Office in June 1965. (Mirrorpix via Getty Images)

"I don't believe for a second that Mike Jeffery was the cause of Jimi's death," he said. "I just don't believe it. The circumstances don't add up. And I was told by so many people that Tappy only wrote that to try and sell books. But I've never believed it. I will never believe it. I was there, and right now I'm probably the last man standing. All the lads are passing. So no, I wouldn't believe that for a second."
Jeffery died in a plane crash near Nantes, France, in 1973.
Jimi Hendrix and Eric Barrett are seen here at the Hollywood Bowl. (Chris Boyd)

Dannemann died in an apparent suicide in 1996, two days after she was found guilty of contempt of court in a long-running legal dispute with Kathy Etchingham, another former girlfriend of Hendrix's. She was 50.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
German painter and former figure skater Monika Dannemann holds a palette and brush as she works on one of her paintings in London, England, circa 1970. (Getty Images)
Barrett said that shortly after Hendrix's death, he lied to reporters about Hendrix's drug use.

"I was, what, 24 when he passed?" said Barrett. "I didn't want to besmirch his memory. So I lied. I just wanted people to see him in a good light. But I came to realize as I got older that I didn't have to lie. Yes, he took drugs. Did he take heroin? I've never seen heroin anywhere near him. I've worked on many backstages for almost 50 years. I know it's a drug that has killed a lot of musicians. But I don't believe Jimi was taking it. He smoked pot. He took a lot of LSD. He took pills. But I don't believe he was into heroin."
Eric Barrett watches over Jimi Hendrix as he performs in Zurich. (Johannes Bruell courtesy of the Marcel Aeby Collection)

Looking back, Barrett described Hendrix as "a wild man" on stage. The musician was famous for playing the guitar behind his head and with his teeth. He would also smash guitars and amps during encores and, on occasion, set his guitar on fire. But when the shows were over and audiences had long since left, Hendrix was a "quiet, mild-mannered, polite young man."
Rock guitarist Jimi Hendrix plays his Fender Stratocaster with his teeth at his last concert on Sept. 6, 1970, on the Isle of Fehmarn, Germany. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)

"He talked to everyone," he said. "He was very charming. And he was shy. People were in awe of Jimi. And when he had his guitar around his neck, over his shoulder, he was comfortable. That was his crutch. But I also remember Paul McCartney walking towards him, and he's gasping, 'It's Paul McCartney!' He was just a shy man who didn't know how to take the accolades of his talent."
"At the Shokan House before Woodstock, trying to teach a very stoned Jimi to ride," said Eric Barrett. (Willis Hogan Jr./David Pearcy Collection)

"I have so many memories of that wonderful man," Barrett continued. "I remember we were all staying in Benedict Canyon and it was my birthday. We were all hanging out by the pool, and Jimi came out in no shirt, just velvet pants. He goes, 'Eric, Eric!' I responded, 'Hey Jimi, what do you need?' He smiled and went, 'Happy birthday, man. Here's some money. Go and buy yourself something you really want.' He gave me $500, which was a huge amount back then."
Jimi Hendrix and Eric Barrett at Benedict Canyon. (Courtesy of Eric Barrett)

"I went to North Beach Leathers, a place I'd seen Jimi had bought some clothes from. I bought myself this long leather coat, spent all my money on it. It was the best gift I ever bought. When I came back, he loved it. He went, 'Wow, that's a coat! I wish I had seen that before you.'"

Rock guitarist Jimi Hendrix performs onstage with his Fender Stratocaster electric guitar at his last concert on Sept. 6, 1970, on the Isle of Fehmarn, Germany. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
Barrett said he carries "beautiful memories" of Hendrix. One in particular has never left him.

"I was on a plane with him after a show," he said. "Jimi looked at me and said, 'Eric, what do you think, will they remember me?' I was flabbergasted. I went, 'Will they remember you? You're huge over here.' But he was so insecure. 'Are you sure, Eric? What if the kids don't come?' I just told him, 'When it comes to success, you have nothing to worry about.' title: Country duo Dan + Shay nearly broke up at height of success when their communication faltered
summary: Dan + Shay reveal the late-night conversation at Dan Smyers' home that saved their partnership after a 2021 communication breakdown nearly ended it all.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Country music duo Dan + Shay revealed they almost went their separate ways at the height of their success.

The duo, composed of Dan Smyers, 39, and Shay Mooney, 34, admitted while on the "Artist Friendly" podcast recently that, at the pinnacle of their success, "there was unhealthy dynamics between both of us 'cause we process things a lot differently."
Mooney explained that their biggest issue was that there "was just a communication stop," and they eventually "got to this point" where it was "just getting really tough."

"We had that moment in 2021, and it was kind of like, all right, do we ride off into the sunset and celebrate our accomplishments or do, like, we have some maybe really hard conversations with each other and fix this?" Mooney said.
The country music duo said they almost broke up at the height of their success. (David Becker/Getty Images)
COUNTRY STAR STEPS AWAY FROM MUSIC TO FOCUS ON HIMSELF AFTER FAME TOOK A TOLL

After host Joel Madden pressed the duo for more details, Smyers explained that, after they landed the opening slot for Kenny Chesney's tour, they were excited but didn't know if they could do it since their relationship was in a bad place.
They ultimately decided, "We have to figure this out," even if it meant that they "call it a day and go out on this Kenny tour as our farewell tour," Smyers said.
The two decided to meet at Smyers' home to have a conversation, with Smyers calling that meeting "the most pivotal critical moment in our entire career."
"We're either going to say peace out to this thing or we're going to figure this out and get it right," Mooney said.
Smyers added, "He ended up staying at the house till like 3, 4 in the morning and just hashing."
The duo had a meeting to discuss how they were going to move forward. (Sebron Snyder/Penske Media via Getty Images)

Mooney later explained that he felt as if Smyers wasn't enjoying himself during the shows, noting that he felt like he didn't "know how to make you enjoy these things" and that he just wanted his friend to be happy.

He was later able to understand that Smyers is particular about "those details that people don't see" and would get upset when things malfunction during shows, for instance, if "the video wall was out," whereas that isn't as big of an issue for Mooney.

"When we finally were like, 'Hey, you're not good at enjoying these things sometimes. I enjoy everything even when it's bad,'" Mooney said. "So, if we can meet somewhere in the middle, we can make this beautiful thing. Which is what happened in the beginning."

In the end, they chose to remain together as a duo after they both apologized for their part in the breakdown of their relationship. Smyers said they also established a new rule by which they let each other know when something is bothering them "rather than letting these things build up and boil and then it just explodes."

title: Comedian Leanne Morgan calls out Hollywood for living in a 'bubble' and misjudging what audiences want to see
summary: Comedian Leanne Morgan says Hollywood lives in a "bubble" and reveals she pushed back on a cursing scene while filming with Reese Witherspoon.
story: Candace Cameron Bure, known for ‘Full House,’ shares her deeply personal faith journey, revealing she embraced Christianity at age 12.
Comedian Leanne Morgan is calling out Hollywood for living in a "bubble."

During a recent appearance on "The Women of Joy Show" podcast, the 60-year-old actress discussed the idea that Christian women don't consume media with host Maegan Waldrep Schwindling, saying they want "quality" content but without "women in their panties shooting bows and arrows and all the things like it."

"Honest to goodness, I think in the secular world, I think people, no, I think a lot of people don't want to see all that," she said. "I think a lot of people don't want to see all that, and I think they're in a bubble out there. And they think people want to see that, but they're not in the middle of the United States."

She gave an example from when she was filming a movie with Reese Witherspoon and Will Ferrell in which she played a Southern mother of four who, in the script, was meant to curse in front of her children.
Morgan called out Hollywood for being in a "bubble." (Dominik Bindl/Getty Images)
FORMER DISNEY STAR DAVID HENRIE REJECTED 'SECULAR' HOLLYWOOD LIFESTYLE AFTER LIFE-CHANGING MONASTERY VISIT

Morgan recalled telling the director that a Southern mother of four "wouldn't talk like that in front of these children." In that case, the director, Nick Stoller, told her, "You know better than I do, Leanne, and you do what you think is best."

"So I think they think in their minds, 'Oh, everybody's talking like this, everybody wants this,' but I don't think the majority of people do," she said. "Or not in the South, especially when you're portraying Southern characters. Or anywhere really."
She also explained that, growing up, no one in her family used swear words and while "it's OK if somebody else wants to use it," she doesn't care to use them herself.
The comedian is now starring in the Netflix show, "Leanne," in which she portrays a Southern mother in her 50s who is rebuilding her life after her husband left her for a younger woman.

She admitted that she felt a "darkness" when she moved to Los Angeles to film her show and that her "boys sent me a Bible study" she could do on her own. Her friend found her a church to attend.

In addition to making sure Southern Christians were not stereotyped on her show, she also felt the pressure to make sure the show was a success, saying she was reminded all the time how much it cost to make the show and how many people were relying on it.
"I've prayed more than I've ever prayed in my life," Morgan said.

title: Hilaria Baldwin explains how she stays fit raising 7 kids with ‘bathroom workouts’ and an unexpected diet
summary: Hilaria Baldwin shares her fitness routine, which includes bathroom workouts, while raising seven kids and pokes fun at Alec Baldwin for not being able to touch his toes.
story: The ‘Nation’s Dumbest’ star tells Fox News Digital how she prioritizes fitness while raising seven kids.
Hilaria Baldwin is taking the phrase "squeeze in a workout" to a whole new level.

The 42-year-old "Nation's Dumbest" contestant and mother of seven told Fox News Digital her fitness routine doesn’t always happen in a gym or even in a dedicated workout space. Sometimes, it happens right there in the bathroom.

"I run every day. … I found being a mom, if I can get 30 minutes of my cardio, it helps my mind. ... It gets me, like, sort of a little bit more regulated with my nervous system, so I really like that," she shared when asked about her go-to workout with a hectic schedule.

And Hilaria isn’t just talking about quick bathroom sweat sessions.
Last month, she gave her fans a front-row look at exactly what those workouts can look like, showing off her physique in a bikini while demonstrating glute exercises in a bathroom.

title: Dolly Parton's path from Nashville newcomer to Billboard's No. 1 country music artist of all time
summary: Dolly Parton gained national attention in 1964 on "The Porter Wagoner Show," later becoming a 10-time Grammy Award winner and Academy Award nominee.
story: Steve Doocy joins 'Fox and Friends' to reflect on the life, career and charitable work of music icon Dolly Parton after her death at age 80. They discuss her music catalog, her Imagination Library literacy program and her Dollywood theme park in Tennessee.
Dolly Parton's career as an entertainer spanned roughly seven decades.
During that time, the legendary country music star cemented herself as an icon not only in the music industry, but also as a movie star and a philanthropist.

From getting her start on "The Porter Wagoner Show" in 1964 to multiple Academy Award nominations, Parton forged a path for herself in the industry and paved the way for female country singers who followed her.
DOLLY PARTON’S SIX-DECADE LOVE STORY WITH CARL DEAN BEGAN AT A LAUNDROMAT
Parton's career as an entertainer spanned roughly seven decades. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
Here are some of Parton's career highlights.
"The Porter Wagoner Show"
Parton joined "The Porter Wagoner Show" in 1967. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
Parton moved to Nashville, Tennessee, in May 1964, the day after graduating from high school, to pursue a career in country music.

Three years later, she released her debut album, "Hello, I'm Dolly," in February 1967, which caught the attention of singer Porter Wagoner. He then invited Parton to join him on his TV show, "The Porter Wagoner Show," a few months later, in September 1967.

Parton's time on the show provided her with national attention and established her as a recording artist. Her duets with Wagoner, starting with "The Last Thing on My Mind," became major country hits. Their partnership also earned Parton her first Grammy nomination in 1970.

In addition to her duets with Wagoner, she released many of her well-known songs during this era, including "Jolene," "Coat of Many Colors," "My Tennessee Mountain Home," "Just Because I'm a Woman" and many more.
After seven years on the show, Parton felt it was time to pursue a solo career, ultimately leaving the show in 1974.
Solo success
Parton left "The Porter Wagoner Show" in 1974 and had a successful solo career. (Getty Images)
Shortly after leaving the show, Parton released "Love Is Like a Butterfly," which quickly climbed to the top of the Billboard country charts.
She continued releasing hit after hit, including "Here You Come Again," off the album with the same name, which earned her first Grammy Award win in 1979.

She had 26 songs reach No. 1 on the Billboard country charts, including "The Bargain Store," "Heartbreaker," "Starting Over Again," "Tennessee Homesick Blues" and "Why'd You Come in Here Lookin' Like That."
In addition to her own music, Parton found success covering other artists' songs in her own style, including "Stairway to Heaven," "The House of the Rising Sun," "Shine" and others.

"Yes, and they loved it. Robert’s been out on tour, so he’s been doing a lot of interviews," she told Hot Press in 2002 about Led Zeppelin singer Robert Plant's reaction to her "Stairway to Heaven" cover.

"And he seems to make mention of it a lot, I guess, because people are asking him about it, and he says something different every time, but he seems to like it. He says he really likes what I did with it, and that makes me feel good."
‘I Will Always Love You’
Parton wrote "I Will Always Love You" in 1973 for her friend, Porter Wagoner. (David Redfern/Redferns)
Parton wrote one of her most well-known songs, "I Will Always Love You," in 1973 when she told Wagoner she wanted to leave the show and go solo.

When Wagoner responded negatively and all her efforts to get him to understand her reasoning fell on deaf ears, Parton thought she would put all her feelings into a song and play it for him to help him understand.

"I said, ‘Porter, sit down. I got something I need to sing to you,’" she told Howard Stern in 2023. "He was just sitting behind his desk and tears started rolling down. He said, ‘That’s just the best song you ever wrote, and you can go if I can produce the song.’"

The song was released in 1974 as part of her "Jolene" album, and climbed to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot Country Singles chart. It returned to No. 1 again in 1982 when Parton released a different version for "The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas."
Whitney Houston's version of the song spent 14 consecutive weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart. (Fotos International/Getty Images)
Nearly two decades after the song's initial release, Whitney Houston's version reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart, where it stayed for 14 consecutive weeks.
Houston recorded an R&B ballad version of the song for the soundtrack to "The Bodyguard."

In addition to staying at the No. 1 spot for 14 weeks, it was Billboard's No. 1 song of 1993, went 19 times platinum in the U.S., and won two Grammy Awards at the 1994 ceremony. This version of the song is also the highest-selling single written by a female artist.
"I almost wrecked, honest to god. I had to pull over to a Walgreens … and listen to the rest of it," Parton told Stern about hearing Houston's version for the first time.
"I couldn’t believe my little country sad song could even be done like that … and it was just overwhelming. That was one of the greatest experiences I ever had in my entire life."
‘Dolly!’ and ‘Dolly’ variety shows
Parton hosted two variety shows of her own, from 1976-1977 and from 1987-1988. (ABC Photo Archives/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)
Two years after leaving "The Porter Wagoner Show," Parton started her own variety show called "Dolly!" in 1976.
The show aired 26 half-hour episodes and featured guest stars such as Kenny Rogers, Linda Ronstadt, Emmylou Harris, Anne Murray and many others.
Ten years after that show ended, she released a second variety show, "Dolly," in 1987.

The show aired 22 one-hour episodes from September 1987 to May 1988 and was a huge ratings success, featuring guests such as Oprah Winfrey, Bruce Willis and Loretta Lynn as well as Kermit the Frog and Miss Piggy.
Iconic collaborations
Parton and Rogers collaborated for the first time in 1983 with "Islands in the Stream." (Beth Gwinn/Redferns)
In addition to Wagoner, Parton had several other significant collaborations throughout her career.

One of her most celebrated partnerships was with Kenny Rogers. The two first connected in 1983 when they recorded the hit song "Islands In the Stream" together. The song was a massive crossover hit and spent two consecutive weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart and earned them a Grammy nomination.
The two later released a joint Christmas album in 1984, "Once Upon a Christmas," and a year later collaborated on "Real Love," which reached No. 1 on Billboard’s Hot Country Singles chart.
Nearly 30 years later, they released "You Can't Make Old Friends" in 2013, the title track of Rogers' album with the same name, earning them another Grammy nomination.
Parton and Rogers reunited in 2013 for their duet "You Can't Make Old Friends." (Rick Diamond)

"It really made me very emotional," Parton told ABC News in September 2013 about the song. "Even when I was recording it, I was tearful, and when I was listening to the demo it really just, you know, it certainly summed us up and our relationship. But it also is such a song of friendship of all kinds."

Parton also partnered with Emmylou Harris and Linda Ronstadt in 1987 to release their highly successful album, "Trio," which largely featured covers, except for "Wildflowers," which was written by Parton for the album.
The album reached No. 1 on Billboard's country albums chart and No. 6 on the Billboard 200 and earned the three artists a Grammy.
They followed it with "Trio II" in 1999, which featured a highly praised cover of Neil Young's song "After the Gold Rush," which earned them yet another Grammy.
Parton also collaborated with Linda Ronstadt and Emmylou Harris on two albums. (Paul Harris/Getty Images)
In addition to these collaborations, Parton released songs with Brad Paisley, Vince Gill, Willie Nelson, Reba McEntire, Miley Cyrus and others.
Movie career
Parton made her feature film debut in 1980 in the comedy "9 to 5." (20th Century Fox/Getty Images)
After making a name for herself in the music world, she set her sights on movies.

Parton made her feature film debut in the 1980 classic comedy "9 to 5," which also starred Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin. Tomlin, Fonda and Parton played a trio of secretaries who took revenge on their sexist boss by kidnapping him and enacting changes in the workplace in his name.
The movie was an instant classic, earning Parton three Golden Globe nominations and an Oscar nomination for best original song for the song she wrote for the film, "9 to 5."

Two years later, Parton made a splash with a second critically-acclaimed role in the film "The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas," playing Miss Mona, a madam at the Chicken Ranch, a long-running Texas brothel.
Dolly Parton also starred in "The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas." (Universal Studios/YouTube)
Her role in the film earned her another Golden Globe nomination.
She then starred in the 1989 movie "Steel Magnolias," alongside Hollywood heavy hitters Sally Field, Shirley MacLaine, Daryl Hannah, Olympia Dukakis and Julia Roberts.
Together, they portrayed a group of Southern women who banded together during life's good and hard moments, with Parton in particular playing a hair stylist.

"I totally related to her. She's not different from me at all, and it wasn't hard for me to play a Southern girl with a Southern accent," she told "Today" in 1989. "And it's not foreign to me, like you said in your intro, for me to do hair, 'cause I grew up doing my sister's hair, my friends' hair. I started cutting and bleaching in a salon on my own at 15 years old and I loved it."
Parton later starred in "Steel Magnolias." (Aaron Rapoport/Corbis/Getty Images)

She also appeared in the films "Rhinestone," "Straight Talk," "The Beverly Hillbillies," "Miss Congeniality 2: Armed and Fabulous," "Joyful Noise" and others, including appearing on three episodes of "Hannah Montana."
Award wins and nominations
Parton won a Grammy for "There Was Jesus" and her first Emmy for "Christmas on the Square" in 2021 at the age of 75. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)
Parton received many accolades during her roughly seven decades in the entertainment industry.

Since releasing her first album in 1967, Parton had received a total of 55 Grammy Award nominations, resulting in 10 wins. Her first win came in 1979 in the female country vocal performance for her song "Here You Come Again."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

She later won awards for "9 to 5," "Trio," "The Grass Is Blue," "Shine" and other projects, with her final nomination coming in 2025 for Best Audiobook Narration and Storytelling Recording for her memoir, "Behind The Seams: My Life In Rhinestones."

Her music was also celebrated in the film world, with two Academy Award nominations for best original song. The first came in 1981 for her song, "9 to 5," and the second in 2006 for the song, "Travelin' Thru," featured in the movie, "Transamerica."
Parton also won 10 CMA Awards, including Entertainer of the Year. (Taylor Hill/Getty Images)

Parton received six Golden Globe nominations over her career, including three for "9 to 5" and one for her performance in "The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas." She also won an Emmy Award for outstanding television movie as an executive producer of "Christmas on the Square."
She also won 10 CMA Awards out of 45 nominations, including Entertainer of the Year in 1978, five ACM Awards and seven CMT Awards.
Recognition
Parton received a Kennedy Center Honor in 2006. (Scott Suchman/WireImage)
Parton was honored in other ways, in addition to the many awards she accumulated throughout her career.
In 1984, the singer received her star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1999 and the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2001.
She later received a Kennedy Center Honor in 2006, recognizing her contributions to American culture.
In 2022, Parton was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Two years later, Billboard named Parton the No. 1 country music artist of all time.
Parton was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images for American Greetings)

"People usually [say] ‘Dolly rocks’ or ‘you rock’ or ‘you’re a rock star.’ I thought they just meant that I was cool, and I took that as a great compliment," she told Billboard in February 2022 about the induction. "But now I’m going to have to take it literally!"
Imagination Library
Parton started the Imagination Library in 1995. (Paul Natkin/Getty Images)
Apart from her work as an entertainer, Parton was also known for her philanthropy.

She started the Imagination Library in 1995, which sends free books to children around the world from birth to age 5, no matter their families' economic status. She was inspired to create the program by her father, who never learned to read or write.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
According to the organization's website, over 3 million kids have registered, and over 330 million books have been gifted since the program started.
"When I was growing up in the hills of East Tennessee, I knew my dreams would come true. I know there are children in your community with their own dreams," Parton said in a statement on the website.

"They dream of becoming a doctor or an inventor or a minister. Who knows, maybe there is a little girl whose dream is to be a writer and singer. The seeds of these dreams are often found in books, and the seeds you help plant in your community can grow across the world."
Dollywood
Parton opened Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tenn., in 1986. (Ron Davis/Getty Images)
Parton showed off her business knowledge when she opened her own theme park called Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, in 1986.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Not only was the theme park popular, drawing about 4 million visitors annually. It also provided job opportunities for thousands of people in the area, proving Parton was all about giving back to her community.

"The Smokies — and the wonderful people who work here — are what make Dollywood so different than many of the other theme parks around the world," she told National Geographic in January 2024, according to People.

"We’re right on the front porch of the most-visited national park in the country, so we take what God gave us and use it to dream up the big dreams we want our guests to experience while they are here riding rides and making memories."
Songs she wrote for others
Parton was a prolific songwriter who wrote songs for other artists often. (Ron Davis/Getty Images)
In addition to her own chart toppers, Parton wrote many songs for other artists that were also big hits.

Included in the list are "Kentucky Gambler," which she wrote for Merle Haggard and became a No. 1 country hit in 1975, and "Put It Off Until Tomorrow" for Bill Phillips, which became a top 10 country hit.

She also wrote "Waltz Me to Heaven" for Waylon Jennings, "The Stranger" for Kenny Rogers," "I'm In No Condition" for Hank Williams Jr., "Love, You’re So Beautiful Tonight" for Willie Nelson and "There'll Always Be Music" for Tina Turner.
These are far from all the songs she wrote. It's been reported that Parton had a catalog of over 3,000 songs penned by her.

title: Meghan Markle's acting U-turn exposes 'lingering problem' after six years of reinventions: experts
summary: Meghan Markle remains in discussions to join "The Gentlemen" for Season 3, raising questions about six years of post-royal reinvention.
story: Dan Wakeford, founder of Celebrity Intelligence, says Meghan Markle could reset her career by finding an extraordinary script and returning to the acting roots that made her famous.
Meghan Markle spent years trying to reinvent herself after leaving royal life, but her latest move could bring her right back to where she started.

With Season 3 of "The Gentlemen" officially greenlit, the Duchess of Sussex remains in talks to join Guy Ritchie's hit drama, People magazine reported, contradicting earlier reports that the potential deal had fallen through. No deal has been finalized, the outlet said.

"If she returns now, it raises the obvious question — what happened to all those other identities she tried on after leaving royal life?" Kinsey Schofield, host of YouTube's "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital.
MEGHAN MARKLE’S ACTING RETURN COULD SPARK FRESH PROBLEMS WITH PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON: EXPERT

On Aug. 24, 2026, People magazine reported that Meghan Markle remained in talks to appear in Netflix's "The Gentlemen" despite reports to the contrary. No deal has been finalized. (Jemal Countess/Getty Images for Time)

"Podcaster, producer, lifestyle entrepreneur, philanthropist, media mogul," said Schofield. "Returning to acting would suggest that the most viable professional identity Meghan has found may ultimately be the one she walked away from."

The talks are in "very early stages," Deadline previously reported. It’s unclear how many episodes she would appear in. The series, which stars Theo James, Kaya Scodelario and Giancarlo Esposito, is filmed in the U.K. and set in England.
Season 2 of "The Gentlemen" premieres Sept. 3, 2026. (Christopher Raphael/Netflix)

Meghan has already dipped her toe back into acting. In 2025, she filmed a small cameo as herself in Amazon MGM Studios' upcoming comedy "Close Personal Friends," starring Brie Larson, Lily Collins, Jack Quaid and Henry Golding. The potential role in "The Gentlemen," however, would mark a more significant return to scripted acting after leaving "Suits."
WATCH: MEGHAN MARKLE COULD REVIVE CAREER WITH SHOCKING ACTING RETURN: EXPERT

"The Gentlemen" follows Eddie Horniman (Theo James), who unexpectedly inherits his father’s title as Duke of Halstead and the family’s sprawling estate after his father dies only to discover that Halstead Manor sits atop a massive cannabis operation and that his reckless older brother has been passed over.

Doug Eldridge, founder of Achilles PR, told Fox News Digital Meghan's potential Hollywood comeback could expose the challenge that has followed her for years of finding an identity once the camera stops rolling that sticks.

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, attends an Invictus Games Friends and Family reception hosted by the City of The Hague and the Dutch Ministry of Defence at Zuiderpark on April 15, 2022, in The Hague, Netherlands. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)
"This has been the lingering problem for Meghan all these years: What is her identity?" he said. "She's ridden a carousel of career horses. Yet for all the rotations, nothing has seemingly stuck."
Meghan Markle starred as Rachel Zane in the legal drama "Suits" before she married Britain's Prince Harry. (Ian Watson/USA Network)

In a statement shared with The New York Times, a spokesperson for the Sussexes said, "On the heels of a wonderful trip with family and friends this summer, Harry and Meghan have decided to spend an extended period in the U.K. this autumn. They are excited to have their children spend more time in the country that’s such an important part of their family’s story."

One of the gates to the Riven Rock neighborhood, where Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, and his wife Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, own a home, is pictured in Montecito, near Santa Barbara, Calif., Aug. 24, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)

The spokesperson confirmed that the couple's business operations will remain based in the U.S. Meghan and Harry will also keep their California home. People magazine reported that Meghan's potential acting project contributed to the couple's decision to return to Britain.
Schofield isn't convinced that filmmakers will now embrace Meghan with open arms.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Royal experts previously told Fox News Digital that Meghan Markle was reportedly eyeing a return to acting after years spent building a new identity outside the royal family. (Tommaso Boddi/Getty Images)
"I'm still skeptical that this represents some grand Hollywood comeback," she said.

"Meghan has spent six years in [California] with a multimillion-dollar Netflix relationship, enormous name recognition and Tyler Perry on speed dial. If acting was genuinely her ambition, she was already standing in arguably the best place in the world to pursue it."
The entrance sign for the gated oceanfront community Montecito Shores is pictured in Montecito near Santa Barbara, Calif., Aug. 24, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)

"That said, 'The Gentlemen' would be a clever choice," she noted. "It's an established hit with a strong creative pedigree, so she wouldn't have to carry the project herself. But first, she has to prove she can disappear into a character rather than have every scene become about Meghan Markle."
The second season of "With Love, Meghan" was released on Netflix on Aug. 26, 2025. (Jake Rosenberg/Netflix)
In 2022, when asked by Variety whether she would ever return to acting, Meghan replied: "I’m done."
"I guess never say never, but my intention is to absolutely not," she said at the time.
Meghan Markle’s return to acting comes after a series of post-royal ventures, including her Netflix lifestyle series, "With Love, Meghan." (Getty Images)
Since stepping back from royal duties in 2020, Meghan has launched a series of ventures with mixed results.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex attends the 2026 Fifteen Percent Pledge Fundraising Gala at Paramount Studios on Feb. 7, 2026, in Los Angeles. (Variety via Getty Images)
Her high-profile Spotify partnership ended in 2023 after her podcast, "Archetypes," produced one season. Her planned Netflix animated series "Pearl" was scrapped before reaching production.

Her lifestyle brand, originally launched as American Riviera Orchard, endured a prolonged rollout before being relaunched to As Ever in 2025. In March 2026, a Sussex spokesperson confirmed that her Netflix lifestyle series, "With Love, Meghan," would continue as seasonal specials rather than return for a third season.

Alysa Nahmias and Meghan Markle, Duchess of Sussex, attend a special screening of Roadside Attractions' "Cookie Queens" at AMC The Grove 14 in Los Angeles July 28, 2026. (Roadside Attractions via Getty Images)
Dan Wakeford, founder of Celebrity Intelligence, told Fox News Digital that, after years of reinvention, Meghan may have little to lose by returning to the career that first put her in the spotlight.
Actress Meghan Markle attends the HBO Luxury Lounge featuring L'Oreal Paris and New Era Cap at the Four Seasons Hotel Los Angeles in Beverly Hills on Jan. 14, 2012. (WireImage)

"The honest picture is more complicated than any of the tabloid headlines and narratives about the empire," he explained. "'With Love, Meghan' became a punchline when it needed to be a launchpad. And when the show was mocked, it poisoned the well for As Ever as well, because the credibility was gone. The problem is that she and Harry believed the big Netflix deals and Spotify checks meant they had leverage when, actually, the checks were the leverage.

"The most interesting path forward for Meghan — and several sources raised this unprompted to Celebrity Intelligence — is a return to acting would actually be a wise move," he continued. "Find an extraordinary script the way Demi Moore did with 'The Substance' and do something that shocks people. Get away from this princess arc and go back to what you loved and what made you famous in the first place."

Demi Moore, winner of Outstanding Performance by a Female Actor in a Leading Role for "The Substance," poses in the press room during the 31st Screen Actors Guild Awards at Shrine Auditorium and Expo Hall in Los Angeles on Feb. 23, 2025. (FilmMagic/Getty Images)

Meghan, daughter of Emmy-winning lighting director Thomas Markle, got her start in Hollywood with bit parts on shows like "Fringe" and "The League." She was also a suitcase model on "Deal or No Deal" before becoming a series regular as Rachel Zane in the legal drama "Suits." She filmed her final scenes in 2017 following her engagement, and her final episode aired in April 2018.
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle attend an official photocall announcing their engagement at The Sunken Gardens at Kensington Palace in London, England, on Nov. 27, 2017. (WireImage/Getty Images)
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"Of all the professional reinventions Meghan has attempted, acting makes the most sense," said Schofield. "She has legitimate experience doing it. She spent years working consistently on 'Suits.' There's nothing embarrassing about returning to the profession that originally made her successful."
Prince Harry, Meghan Markle, Katharine McPhee and David Foster posed for a photo at the legendary music producer's charity event. (Vito Amati/The David Foster Foundation via Getty Images)

"What I find amusing is the contradiction," she said. "Meghan spent years presenting herself as though acting was something she had evolved beyond. Perhaps the great reinvention is discovering that the original brand worked better than all the rebrands."
Actress Meghan Markle visits AOL Studios in New York City March 17, 2016. (FilmMagic/Getty Images)

Stepping back in front of the camera could work in Meghan’s favor. Recent polls have placed both Harry and Meghan near the bottom of the royal family’s popularity rankings in Britain, ahead of only former Prince Andrew, People magazine reported.
But if there's one thing Meghan has consistently proven, it's her ability to command attention, the enduring power of the so-called "Markle Sparkle."
Meghan Markle on the red carpet for "Suits," circa 2015. (Mike Coppola/NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images)

"Meghan brings something you cannot manufacture with a marketing budget, and that's global curiosity," said Schofield. "Love her or loathe her, people will watch the first episode just to see whether she can still act. Every photograph from the set becomes international news. Every trailer gets dissected. Every interview generates headlines.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Meghan Markle attends the Womenswear Spring-Summer 2026 show during Paris Fashion Week on Oct. 5, 2025, in Paris, France. (Andrea Cremascoli/Getty Images)

"From a publicity standpoint, I completely understand why a producer might take that gamble," she said. "The question is whether the spectacle surrounding Meghan ultimately serves the story or overwhelms it. But there's an enormous difference between attracting attention and building a sustainable career. The real test is whether anybody wants to see Meghan's character again once the novelty wears off."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: 'Veronica Mars' star Jason Dohring traded Hollywood for farming
summary: Jason Dohring told his agents he was going to farm, and now the "Veronica Mars" star runs an 11-acre regenerative farm in Florida with his family.
story: The 53-year-old actor was on a tractor the first time he spoke with "Ransom Canyon" showrunner, April Blair.
"Veronica Mars" star Jason Dohring has stepped away from acting to focus on a new passion.

During a recent appearance on the "Don't Do Nothing" podcast, the 44-year-old actor shared that he developed an interest in gardening around four years ago and told his agents, "I'm just going to go farm for a minute."

"I just got an interest in it and I've kind of the last three years I built like, I'm on my third farm now and we're just making great food for people cause I really realized that people are getting sick from the food that they're eating," he said.

He first began planting in Los Angeles, before developing a 14-acre farm in West Virginia, where they planted 4,000 trees, including apples, cherries, pears, peaches and nectarines, noting he probably planted "3,500 of them myself."
Dohring said he became interested in farming a few years ago, and has since developed three farms. (Getty Images)
'THE THORN BIRDS' STAR RACHEL WARD TRADED 'EMPTY' HOLLYWOOD FOR FARM LIFE IN AUSTRALIA

The actor now lives on an 11-acre farm in Florida with his wife, Lauren Kutner, and their four kids, noting he moved there because of the weather. He said that when farming in California, they weren't allowed to drill a well and would run out of water.

"L.A. is crazy. [You can go] eight, nine months with no rain. You know what I mean?" he said. "That's when I when we moved to Florida I was like we get infinite rain. We have infinite manure. Like you know you could farm for free."

title: Former Disney Channel star alleges she was sexually abused at 14 after being told to ‘bond’ with employee

story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
A former Disney Channel star made disturbing allegations about her time on set in a new lawsuit.
Raquel Lee Bolleau claimed an adult male employee sexually abused her when she was just 14 after Disney personnel allegedly encouraged her to "bond" with him.
The alleged abuse began during production of the 2001 Disney Channel movie "The Poof Point," after personnel directed her to spend time with the adult employee.
FORMER DISNEY STAR MAITLAND WARD SAYS YOUNG ACTORS WERE TREATED LIKE A 'PRODUCT' IN HOLLYWOOD FACTORY
According to the complaint obtained by Fox News Digital, the man supplied the 14-year-old with alcohol and repeatedly sexually assaulted her during filming.
After the alleged sexual assault, Bolleau recalled the employee telling her, "You're old enough. You can handle it."

Former Disney Channel star Raquel Lee Bolleau sued The Walt Disney Company, alleging an adult male Disney employee repeatedly sexually assaulted her when she was 14 while filming the 2001 movie "The Poof Point." (Michael Tran/AFP)

Bolleau claimed she returned to set smelling of alcohol, vomiting and visibly changed after the alleged assault, but Disney personnel failed to investigate how a 14-year-old got alcohol or seek medical care for her. Instead, the complaint claimed, an executive branded her "out of control," said the movie had gone "haywire" and told her representatives Disney was "extremely upset."

On another occasion, an on-set Disney executive producer allegedly repeatedly told Bolleau she "need[ed] Jesus" and told her mother, "your daughter has a demon inside her," according to the complaint.
Bolleau alleged Disney repeatedly separated her from her guardian despite California protections requiring a guardian of a performer under 16 remain within "sight or sound" of the child.

According to the complaint, her guardian could not watch Bolleau while she filmed or accompany her to wardrobe and makeup, and production personnel once told the guardian, "We do not even need you on set." Bolleau claimed those practices left her without adequate adult supervision and gave her alleged abuser unrestricted access to her.

Bolleau alleged the employee also sexually harassed and touched her in front of others on set. Bolleau alleged sound technicians could hear many of the comments, but no one intervened or asked what the adult employee was saying to her.

"Instead of protecting and supporting its minor employee who was being repeatedly raped, sexually assaulted, sexually abused, and harassed, Disney covered up Mr. Doe’s abuse, and blamed Ms. Bolleau for the impact of Mr. Doe’s horrific misconduct," Bolleau's lawyers wrote.

"Disney’s egregious role in Mr. Doe’s abuse of Ms. Bolleau is part of a broader, institutional, and systemic pattern of institutional and individual failures at Disney that extends far beyond 'The Poof Point.'"

Bolleau claimed the alleged abuse continued after filming wrapped. According to the complaint, Disney booked Bolleau in first class while seating her guardian in economy on the flight back to California.

Bolleau alleged the employee told her to sit next to him and bring a blanket to cover them before sexually assaulting her during the flight and continuing until their row began to deboard at Los Angeles International Airport.

title: Country singer Lauren Alaina credits small-town Georgia roots for strong work ethic, faith

story: When speaking with Fox News Digital, Alaina said she comes "from a long line of hardworking people and believers" who taught her the importance of "working hard and having a strong faith."
Country singer Lauren Alaina is thankful for her small town roots and the lessons they taught her.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the 31-year-old singer spoke about her upcoming album, "Stages," and shared why she credits growing up in Rossville, Georgia for her success and her work ethic.

"I come from a long line of hardworking people and believers and dreamers in their own way, whatever their path was," she said. "Mine obviously looked very different than the rest of my family because my working hard and my dreaming was leaving home and going to a new place, which people don't do a ton in Rossville, Georgia."

title: Dolly Parton defied country music's expectations for women and built a career on her own terms: experts
summary: Dolly Parton broke barriers for women in country music by controlling her image, owning her work and refusing to shed her femininity for authority.
story: Fox News senior national correspondent William La Jeunesse goes through the legacy of country music legend Dolly Parton on 'The Story.'

From the get-go, Dolly Parton was a force to be reckoned with. She challenged social norms, broke barriers for women in country music and ultimately helped redefine what a female country star could be.

Throughout her life, Parton — who died Aug. 25 after a brief battle with cancer — helped "expand the narrative" of how women were perceived, not only in country music but beyond it, experts told Fox News Digital.

"Dolly followed some other pioneering women like Patsy Cline and Loretta Lynn who had already challenged expectations and proved that women’s experiences belonged in country music," Dr. Tracy King, a chartered clinical psychologist, writer and pop-culture commentator, told Fox News Digital.
DOLLY PARTON DIES AT THE AGE OF 80: A LOOK AT HER LIFE THROUGH PHOTOS
Dolly Parton paved the way for women in country music and beyond. (ABC Photo Archives/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

"However, where they belonged was still within a narrow narrative of specific roles such as: the respectable woman, the suffering wife, the attractive female or the supporting partner to a more ‘powerful’ man."

"Dolly helped expand the narrative," King continued. "She could be the glamorous star, serious songwriter, ambitious decision-maker, owner of her work and a brand manager of her public identity all at the same time. She did not have to remove her femininity, accent or background to become powerful."
WHY DOLLY PARTON COULD BRING TOGETHER AMERICANS WHO AGREE ON ALMOST NOTHING

"This gave other women much more possibility," she added. "You could be emotionally open without being seen as weak, commercially ambitious without being masculine and visible without surrendering control of your story."
Dolly Parton died on Aug. 25. (AP Photo/Andres Kudacki, File)
Long before the rhinestones, platinum records and entertainment empire, Parton was one of 12 children raised in a one-room cabin in rural Tennessee, where money was scarce but music was a constant.
"I’ll always be a country musician because I’m a country girl," she told People in 1975. "My style is my soul and my feelings. I’ll tell the world in my songs what I wouldn’t have told my mother."
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Parton would eventually turn the struggles and values of her childhood into the foundation of her songwriting.
Country singer Dolly Parton was one of 12 children. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
STEVE DOOCY: THE DOLLY PARTON I SAW WHEN THE CAMERAS STOPPED ROLLING

"Dolly refused to treat the things that made her different as problems that needed correcting," King said. "Her appearance became instantly recognizable, her voice very distinct and her background became central to the stories she told."

"She did not deny the poverty of her childhood, but she refused to accept that it made her inferior," King continued. "In ‘Coat of Many Colors,’ the homemade coat for which she was mocked also represented her mother’s love. Dolly acknowledged the shame and hurt, but she didn’t allow the cruelest interpretation of that experience to become the only one."
DOLLY PARTON’S SIX-DECADE LOVE STORY WITH CARL DEAN BEGAN AT A LAUNDROMAT

"This is what it means to reclaim your story," she added. "We cannot always prevent other people from judging us, but we can refuse to let their judgment become our identity. Her accent and background also helped create trust. People felt that she remembered where she came from and had not reinvented herself by rejecting her earlier life. She became successful without treating the person she had once been as someone who needed to disappear."
Parton was proud of her upbringing and used her values as a stepping stone into building her empire. (WireImage)
But Parton’s roots weren’t the only thing she refused to shed on her way to the top.
The Grammy Award winner leaned heavily into her trademark appearance — refusing to accept the idea that femininity and authority were mutually exclusive.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"Dolly understood the assumptions people made about her appearance and used humor to demonstrate that she knew exactly what they were thinking," King said. "She was in on the joke, but she was never the joke."
Parton "consciously created her image" rather than allowing the industry to create it for her, King said.
DOLLY PARTON REFUSED TO PICK POLITICAL SIDES FOR DECADES: ‘I’M NOT IN POLITICS, I’M AN ENTERTAINER’

"The contrast between that image and her intelligence made other people’s prejudice visible," she said. "It exposed the judgers. Women are still frequently told that authority must look restrained, serious and almost masculine. Dolly rejected that. She did not change her appearance to prove she was intelligent; she made her intelligence impossible to deny and that femininity could run alongside and did not have to be denied."
Parton’s carefully constructed image didn’t prevent her from earning respect.
It became part of what made her success so significant.
Parton was known for her trademark appearance. (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Na)
TRUMP MOURNS DOLLY PARTON, ORDERS US FLAGS LOWERED NATIONWIDE AFTER COUNTRY MUSIC ICON DIES
Professor Susan McClary, a professor of music at Case Western Reserve University, said Parton entered the industry with "two strikes against her" — only to turn both into strengths.

"When Dolly Parton began her career, she had two strikes against her: she performed country music — a genre disdained by many listeners; and she presented herself in her attire and make-up as a cartoonish stereotype," McClary said. "Through perseverance, talent, self-deprecating sense of humor, and generosity, she managed to win over a vast fanbase while never compromising her values."
"Feminists who might have dismissed her appearance came to see her as a role model who insisted on creating and maintaining her own image," McClary said.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Parton passed away after a brief battle with cancer. (Shirlaine Forrest/WireImage)

But Parton’s determination to control her own identity extended far beyond her looks. Behind the larger-than-life image was a savvy songwriter and businesswoman who was equally determined to control her own work.

"Dolly built on the groundwork of Kitty Wells, Patsy Cline, Loretta Lynn and Tammy Wynette and expanded the range of what a female country performer could become," King said. "She opened the door to women being recognized as authors of their careers rather than being selected and managed by men. She wrote her own material, protected her publishing rights, left a successful partnership with a powerful male performer and developed businesses beyond the control of the traditional Nashville system."
"She showed younger artists that creative freedom depends not only on being heard, but on retaining ownership and decision-making power," she added.
Parton also demonstrated that female country artists did not have to remain confined to what society expected of them.
Parton paved the way for female country stars such as Reba McEntire, Shania Twain and more. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

"A female country artist could enter pop music, film and television, establish a production company, build businesses and still remain connected to country music," King said. "We can see elements of that broader template in the careers of performers such as Reba McEntire, Shania Twain, Faith Hill, Trisha Yearwood, The Chicks, Carrie Underwood, Miranda Lambert, Taylor Swift and Kacey Musgraves."

"Her songwriting opened another door by showing that women’s inner lives could carry major commercial songs," King added. "Female characters could be jealous, angry, ambitious, sexually judged, economically exploited, ashamed, heartbroken or ready to leave. Later female performers had greater permission to write from their own point of view rather than to present a version of womanhood that was comfortable for a male audience."
Parton’s influence ultimately stretched far beyond music.
Parton was proud of her charitable work through the Dollywood Foundation and Imagination Library. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images for American Greetings)

She built a business empire centered in her home state of Tennessee, with Dollywood becoming one of the state’s most recognizable attractions. Her charitable work through the Dollywood Foundation and Imagination Library left another lasting mark.

The Imagination Library, inspired by Parton’s father, who never learned to read or write, provides free books to children from birth to age 5. The program grew into an international literacy initiative, distributing millions of books to children around the world.
Following Parton’s death, tributes poured in from some of the women who followed the path she helped widen.

"Dolly, thank you for all the wonderful things you did for us here on earth," Reba McEntire wrote on Instagram. "Your love, your music and you gave so much with your huge huge heart. There will never ever be another you. We will remember and cherish every memory and every note you ever played and sang."
"Thank you, Lord, for Dolly," she concluded. "She’s gonna have a blast in heaven singing all her favorite songs with all her family and friends who have gone on before her."
Shania Twain also shared an emotional tribute, calling Parton her "mentor."

"Dolly was pure light sent from heaven," Twain wrote on Instagram. "My mentor is gone. My songwriting teacher and hero of grace and humility. There is a hole in my heart but the joy of just the thought of her smile will continue to fill me with inspiration for as long as I live."
Parton left a "blueprint" for female country artists. (Getty Images)
Decades after she first entered an industry with narrow expectations for female performers, Parton left women in country music with far more room to define success on their own terms, said King.

"Dolly left female performers with a much wider blueprint: write the story, own the work, control your own narratives and shake off the ones anyone else may have given you," King said.

title: Why Dolly Parton’s death can feel like losing someone you knew personally
summary: Fans worldwide describe "post-Parton depression" as Dolly Parton's death triggers intense parasocial grief that psychologists say mirrors real loss.
story: Dolly Parton, the Grammy-winning singer, songwriter and philanthropist whose career spanned over six decades, has died at 80.
The death of Dolly Parton has prompted an outpouring of grief from fans around the world, many of whom have shared that they feel like they’ve lost someone they knew personally.

Grief experts say it’s possible to experience genuine feelings of loss even if there wasn’t a personal relationship — particularly when the public figure has become woven into people’s memories and routines over a long period of time.
Psychologists refer to this type of loss as parasocial grief, according to licensed clinical psychologist Dr. Dara Houp.
DOLLY PARTON’S PRIVATE CANCER BATTLE HIGHLIGHTS WHY SOME PATIENTS DON’T SHARE THEIR DIAGNOSES

"When a celebrity shares their personal life – childhood experiences, hardships and victories – our brains register these bits of information through the same emotional and neural pathways utilized for our real-life friendships and a genuine attachment is developed," Houp, with Pathways Psychological Services in New York City, told Fox News Digital.
When that perceived relationship comes to an end, people may experience the parasocial grief, she said.

\Fans of Dolly Parton visit a mural featuring her likeness in the city's North Side on Aug. 26, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. Fans across the nation are mourning the death of the country music star, actress and philanthropist who died on Tuesday at age 80. (Getty Images)

Desiree Taranto, a licensed mental health counselor and clinical director at Empower Your Mind Therapy in New York City, said the widespread reaction also reflects "collective grief," a shared emotional response when a loss resonates across a community.
"Parton’s music, movies, philanthropy and public persona became part of many people’s family traditions, memories and difficult life moments," she told Fox News Digital.
Fans share their grief

"I honestly didn’t know I could react that way over someone I don’t even personally know," one user wrote in a grief support group on Reddit. "[Dolly] was a ray of sunshine in this dark world nowadays, and I just can’t help but cry and get so emotional about it."
Another user shared that "as each day passes, losing Dolly seems to hurt more instead of less. I have found myself crying and feeling this deep sadness that I just can’t shake."
IN WAKE OF DOLLY PARTON'S DEATH, ONCOLOGIST REVEALS WHY SOME PATIENTS KEEP CANCER DIAGNOSES SECRET
"I never met Dolly, and I know she didn’t know me, but I loved her for most of my life. That love was real, and so this grief feels real too."
Someone else in a different group referred to the feelings of sadness as "post-Parton depression."
Fans honor Dolly Parton with flowers, notes and small gifts at the site of her star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame on Aug. 26, 2026 in Hollywood, California. (Getty Images)
"I don't know why I am taking Dolly Parton's death so hard," one user wrote. "I never met her… She didn't know me. But for some reason, I can't stop crying."
"I think the reason it's hard is because she was a light and just a wonderful human," someone else shared. "She is exactly who Jesus wanted us to be."
Why does it feel personal?
The emotions people experience when grieving a celebrity can feel as real as those felt after losing someone they knew personally, Houp said.

"Perceived relational intimacy, not whether we actually know an individual, is largely what determines the intensity of grief," she said. "The emotional connection your brain developed runs along the same neural pathways as real-life bonds."
"Accept your feelings and know that it is okay to mourn someone you never met."

It’s also possible that the deaths of certain celebrities — particularly those associated with childhood, family traditions or major life moments — are more likely to trigger an intense grief response, the expert noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"When a celebrity’s life is connected to a personal milestone — such as a break-up or the birth of a child — their death permanently disrupts a living connection to who, what or where you used to be," Houp said. "Losing a celebrity can feel like losing a piece of your own history."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
A song may be tied to someone who has died, a family memory or a difficult period when Parton’s work brought comfort, Taranto noted, making the loss feel connected to a person’s own life story.
Over decades in the public eye, Parton gave fans a window into her life, allowing them to form a sense of who she was, Houp said.
Fans pay tribute to Dolly Parton at her home in Brentwood on Aug. 25, 2026 in Brentwood, Tennessee. (Getty Images)
"For many who followed Dolly’s life, she represented resilience and ambition, authenticity and bold self-expression, and a rare, unconditional kindness," she said.
"We identified with the goodness we saw in Dolly and felt encouraged by her ability to overcome hardship – thereby furthering our sense of connection to her."
Tips to navigate grief
Taranto offered advice for those feeling the grief following Parton’s death.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Accept your feelings and know that it is okay to mourn someone you never met," she said. "Do not judge yourself or feel embarrassed because that person’s work, values or advocacy touched your life personally."
It can also help to reach out to others who are also grieving the loss.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Be there for each other and allow others to be there for you," Taranto advised. "Tell stories, listen to her music, watch her movies or journal about what she meant to you."
"Remember the positive impact she made in the world and the ways she used her platform for good. Shared grief can help us process a loss because it reminds us that we are not alone in it."

title: Drug institute warns that Trump-shaped ecstasy pills contain potentially fatal ingredient
summary: The Trimbos Institute in the Netherlands issued a red alert after Donald Trump-shaped ecstasy pills containing potentially fatal PMMA were handed in at testing centers.
story: President Donald Trump highlighted a massive drop in fentanyl deaths and illegal drugs entering the country by sea in an exclusive interview with Trace Gallagher.
A respected drug treatment and mental health center in the Netherlands issued a warning against taking ecstasy pills shaped like President Donald Trump’s head, saying they could be fatal.

The Trimbos Institute warned in a "red alert" that the pills contain a high concentration of PMMA, also known as para-methoxymethamphetamine, which is similar to ecstasy’s active ingredient MDMA but is slower acting.
The slow onset could encourage users to take more and potentially overdose.
The institute shared a photo of two of the pills, one of which was green on the front and the other yellow. They were red and blue on the back.
POLICE SEIZE COCAINE BRICKS WITH STICKERS OF NORWEGIAN SOCCER STAR ERLING HAALAND ALL OVER THEM

This undated photo provided by the Trimbos Institute of Mental Health and Addiction shows pills with a depiction of President Donald Trump on one side and NL and Trump stamped on the other. (Trimbos Institute of Mental Health and Addiction via AP)
The pills had a likeness of Trump’s face on the front and the name "Trump" and letters "NL" on the back.
"Absolutely do not use these pills," the institute said.
In 2018, Indiana State police seized orange Trump-shaped ecstasy pills in an operation targeting small-time drug traffickers.
Those pills also had Trump’s face on the front and "great again" written on the back, an apparent reference to his Make America Great Again slogan.
The institute said the pills have a slow-acting ingredient that could lead to overdose. (Trimbos Institute of Mental Health and Addiction via AP)
In 2017, German police also seized thousands of Trump-shaped ecstasy pills, which also appeared to be orange, that had an estimated street value of nearly $46,000.
There have yet to be any reports of overdoses or deaths due to the drug, spokesperson Anniek Groothuis told The Associated Press.
GERMAN POLICE SEIZE THOUSANDS OF 'TRUMP' ECSTASY TABLETS
"We do not know of any victims where PMMA was found in their blood," she said.
Indiana State Police released a photo showing ecstasy pills bearing President Trump's image and the words "great again" in 2018. (Indiana State Police )
The clinic said the pills had recently been handed in to some of its centers where it tests drugs before people take them.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
While ecstasy is illegal in the Netherlands, hundreds of thousands of people use the drug every year, according to the government.
Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

title: ‘Quiet quitting’ in marriage: The subtle signs a spouse has emotionally checked out
summary: Licensed therapist Lisa Brookes Kift outlines how "quiet quitting" erodes marriages and why the absence of arguing may signal emotional detachment.
story: Dr. Anna Elton discusses why stressed partners may lose interest in physical affection and how regular check-ins, gratitude and intentional time together can change the dynamic at home.
"Quiet quitting," a workplace term for doing only the minimum required, has also been used to describe a pattern in some marriages.
In relationships, the informal term refers to spouses who remain together while reducing their emotional effort, communication or involvement in the relationship.
Couples may continue managing day-to-day responsibilities, such as household tasks and parenting, even as one partner becomes emotionally and physically disengaged, relationship experts say.
‘NO CONTACT’ ON THE RISE: NEARLY 2 IN 5 AMERICANS CUT TIES WITH LOVED ONES
Discussion of the term has gained traction on social media, with users sharing videos and posts about remaining in a marriage while feeling checked out.
Licensed marriage and family therapist Lisa Brookes Kift of Marin Therapy and Counseling in California told Fox News Digital that a noticeable absence of friction can be an early warning sign.
A couple lying in bed and looking at their cellular phones, ignoring each other (iStock)

"It’s a myth that an absence of arguing in a relationship automatically means the relationship is healthy," Kift said. "Many are conflict-avoidant and rather than address their feelings, opt to sweep them under the rug, which over the long term erodes the foundation of emotional safety."
Kift said a person’s attachment style — patterns of seeking closeness and support in relationships — can influence how they respond to marital distress.
CUT OFF BY YOUR ADULT CHILD? PSYCHOLOGY RESEARCHER REVEALS WHAT PARENTS SHOULD DO NEXT
"An avoidant style may be more able to stay in their own lane — on their own island — to ride it out, because they are most comfortable resourcing in themselves," she said.

Those with a more secure attachment style are less likely to stay in that dynamic because they may be more inclined to give a partner the benefit of the doubt and believe problems can be worked through, the expert noted.
Early lessons about trust, worthiness and whether personal needs will be met heavily influence how a partner handles marital distress. (bymuratdeniz via Getty Images)
These patterns can be shaped, in part, by early experiences involving trust, worthiness and whether a person’s emotional needs were met, according to Kift.
"What did they learn about whether their needs would be met? Whether the most important people to them could be trusted? That they were lovable for who they were and not what they did?" Kift asked.
When adult relationships appear to repeat those early disappointments, partners can lose hope, she added.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"I’ve seen quite a few people in my therapy practice who have taken this stance, where there have been failed attempts to get emotional and other needs met, leading to hopelessness," Kift said.
Kift identified several early signs that a partner may be becoming emotionally disengaged.
Decline in open communicationUnresolved conflictsGrowing impatienceA tendency to assume the worst about a spouse's intentions rather than giving them the benefit of the doubt

Left unaddressed, the relationship could shift into what journalist Monica Corcoran Harel described on Oprah’s podcast as "parallel play," a reference to toddlers playing side by side without meaningfully engaging with one another.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Repairing a marriage requires both partners to reengage, Kift said, which can be difficult once one spouse has become deeply emotionally detached.
Signs like reduced communication, unresolved arguments, growing impatience and assuming the worst about a partner’s intentions can signal an impending emotional slide. (iStock)

"If one has fully checked out, they will not be open to repair," she said, adding that hypervigilance — remaining on guard for hurt or disappointment — can make it difficult for a person to recognize positive changes in their partner.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
For couples willing to work on the relationship, Kift suggests starting with a conversation that feels safe and communicates care.

As one example, she suggested saying, "I know it may not have looked like it, but you and our marriage are very important to me. Can we find a time to sit down and talk?"
