title: At least 1 dead, over a dozen missing at Grand Canyon after extreme flash flooding
summary: Authorities are searching for hikers and campers who may have been trapped in the area.
story: At least one person is dead and more than a dozen others are missing or unaccounted for after flash floods overwhelmed a remote area of the Grand Canyon, including a historic lodge near the bottom of the site, park officials said Sunday afternoon.

The National Park Service is asking for information about anyone who may have been hiking or backpacking along Bright Angel Creek in Arizona, as well as campers with plans to stay at Phantom Ranch or the Bright Angel Campground.
Officials are also trying to track down travelers who might have been stranded along the North Kaibab Trail.

The National Park Service said in an evening update that a 46-year-old man was recovered from Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River. The Coconino County Medical Examiner’s Office was at the scene, the NPS said.
The park service earlier Sunday said 15 people were missing or unaccounted for, down from a previous estimate of 20.
As of Sunday morning, 62 people had been evacuated from Phantom Ranch and the lower North Kaibab Trail. Additional evacuations from Phantom Ranch and the Cottonwood Campground were expected.

Park administrators also said that footbridges along Bright Angel Creek were destroyed, “eliminating hiker access across the creek,” and that certain Colorado River crossings were closed while damage is assessed.

“The flash flood resulted in significant impacts to infrastructure throughout Bright Angel Canyon,” the National Park Service said in a statement. “Grand Canyon National Park staff are continuing to assess damage to trails, bridges, utilities, facilities and other infrastructure.”
Phantom Ranch is accessible only by hiking, raft or mule transport. It has been a coveted Grand Canyon destination since it opened in 1922.
Colorado River traffic was also shut down because of the risk of floating debris.

title: Dolly Parton’s niece shares emotional tribute after singer’s private funeral
summary: The country star’s funeral Friday was a private affair attended by family members, said her niece Lainey Parton.
story: Dolly Parton was laid to rest in a private funeral service attended by family on Friday, according to her niece.

Lainey Parton shared an emotional tribute post on Instagram on Saturday, writing: “This is a really hard post for me to make. I wanted to wait until after my granny was laid to rest yesterday before I tried to put any of this into words.”
Parton died Tuesday following a brief battle with cancer at age 80. Her social media pages said that at her request, a small private service would be held for immediate family.
Lainey remembered Parton as a loving and inspiring figure who “believed in me before I even knew how to believe in myself.”
“Because she couldn’t have kids of her own, she always made us feel like we were hers. She loved us that way, and I’ll forever be grateful for that,” she wrote.
Lainey shared a slew of photos from growing up with Parton, some from childhood and others taken onstage with the country star.
Lainey recalled singing with Parton on her 2024 “Smoky Mountain DNA” album, which included various Parton family members.

“I was a freshman in high school and SO nervous. But she had a way of making me feel like nothing bad could happen. She made me feel safe, confident, and like I belonged right there beside her,” Lainey recalled.
She said the music icon backed her decision to attend beauty school and helped her fund it.
“She didn’t just tell me to chase my dreams, she helped me get there,” she said.

“I’m so thankful I said yes to the opportunities and memories I got to share with her as my Aunt Dolly, including being in a movie with her. I’m so glad I have those moments to look back on now. I have things I can watch, hear, and hold onto when I miss her,” she continued.
While the family — and the world beyond — mourns Parton’s passing, Lainey said she’s holding on to the precious memories she shared with her “granny.”

“It still doesn’t feel real that she’s gone. I’m going to miss her voice, her laugh, her hugs, and just knowing she was there. I’m even going to miss those 4 AM calls, and I’d give anything to see her name pop up on my phone again,” she said.

“I feel incredibly lucky that I got to call her my granny. Thank you for always believing in me, loving me, and making me feel like I could do anything. I love you, Granny. Always,” she said, concluding her post.

The “Jolene” singer hailed from rural Tennessee, born into a large but tight-knit family. She was one of 12 children, and as her own family expanded, Parton maintained an incredibly close relationship with her siblings, nieces and nephews.

Her death sparked widespread mourning and emotional tributes from her fans, Hollywood and the music industry. The 11-time Grammy-winning singer-songwriter was more than just an artist. She was an icon who transcended genre and time, a philanthropist focused on children and poverty, and a businesswoman.
Parton was preceded in death by her husband of 59 years, Carl Thomas Dean, who died in 2025, and her parents, Avie Lee Caroline Owens and Robert Lee Parton Sr.

title: New Mexico man accused of fatally shooting cousin after argument over enchiladas
summary: Police say the men had been drinking and arguing before a fistfight broke out. A witness said the victim was walking away when Ervin Gutierrez pulled a gun and opened fire.
story: A New Mexico man is accused of fatally shooting his cousin after an evening of drinking escalated from an argument over enchiladas into a fistfight, according to an arrest warrant.
Ervin Joaquin Gutierrez, 22, is charged with an open count of murder in the Aug. 27 killing of Nathaniel Cavazos at an apartment complex in Albuquerque.

Gutierrez was arrested by Albuquerque police Friday evening and booked into the Metropolitan Detention Center shortly after midnight Saturday, according to jail records. He is being held on an open count of murder.

Albuquerque police responded to a shooting shortly before 11 p.m. and found Cavazos unresponsive in a pool of blood on the walkway between apartment buildings. He had been shot at least once and died from his injuries, according to the warrant affidavit.

A cousin of both men who told police he witnessed the shooting said Gutierrez had arrived earlier that afternoon to visit. The three later bought groceries, returned to the apartment and cooked green enchiladas while drinking alcohol, according to the affidavit.

The witness told authorities tension began when Gutierrez repeatedly claimed the chile on his enchiladas was hotter than the chile on Cavazos’ plate and challenged him to eat some. Cavazos responded that they had all eaten the same enchiladas, so the chile should be equally hot. The men continued arguing after the witness suggested they take his dog for a walk.

Eventually, Cavazos punched Gutierrez, and the two fought, according to the witness’ account. Cavazos struck Gutierrez enough to leave him bleeding before the fight ended and Cavazos began walking away, according to the affidavit.
Gutierrez then allegedly pulled out a handgun and confronted Cavazos, saying, “We’re family! We’re family! How could you do this to me?” the witness told investigators.
The witness said Cavazos was about 10 feet away and was not holding a weapon when Gutierrez fired three or four times, striking him in the back. Gutierrez then fled, according to the affidavit.
Police said the witness showed investigators a Snapchat message in which Gutierrez allegedly said Cavazos had threatened his life.
“Is he really dead?” Gutierrez allegedly wrote. “I did not want to kill him but i didn’t want him to kill me.”
Investigators said a handgun belonging to Cavazos was found at least 10 yards from his body.

title: College football player dies after collapsing on sideline moments after scoring touchdown
summary: William Jewell College in Missouri didn’t disclose the nature of junior running back MicahJo Barnett’s medical emergency.
story: A running back for William Jewell College in Missouri died Saturday after suffering a medical emergency during the first quarter of his team’s season opener, shortly after scoring a touchdown.
MicahJo Barnett, a junior business administration major at the Division II school, had a health crisis on the sideline following the score, according to a statement released by the college.
The home game against Fort Lewis College at Greene Stadium in Liberty, Missouri, was canceled after the incident.
Neither William Jewell athletics nor the NCAA, which also released a statement on Barnett’s death, disclosed the nature of his medical emergency.
Barnett was a Liberty native who played at Liberty North High School, where he helped lead the team to a state championship in 2023, according to records.

“Micah’s life was taken far too soon, leaving his family, friends, teammates, and community heartbroken,” read a message on a GoFundMe page set up for his family by one of his former youth coaches. The post described Barnett as “a talented and kind young man who was loved by so many.”

title: Rep. Jim Clyburn says impeaching Trump shouldn’t be Democrats’ priority if they win back the House
summary: The South Carolina representative also told “Meet the Press” that he regretted his support for Clarence Thomas during his Supreme Court confirmation hearings in 1991.
story: Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., said Sunday that Democrats should not prioritize impeaching President Donald Trump if they win control of the House in the upcoming midterm elections, but instead should focus on making life more affordable for Americans.

Clyburn told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that if Democrats take back the House, he feels confident that their first order of business would be making the country accessible and affordable for all citizens.

Pressed on whether he believes Democrats should rule out the prospect of impeaching Trump if they regain control of the House, the South Carolina lawmaker said, “I don’t rule it out, but I don’t rule it in.”

“I don’t think that should be our priority if we get into office,” he added. “Our priority ought to be making housing, education, energy, healthcare affordable and accessible for all of our citizens. Impeaching the president will not do that.”
His remarks come days after House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., was asked a similar question by CNN and said that he wasn’t ruling out impeaching Trump.

“We haven’t ruled anything in and we haven’t ruled anything out,” Jeffries told CNN, adding that he’s leaving those decisions up to the Democrats who would be in charge of the House Oversight and Judiciary committees if Democrats take back the House.

“As we’ve done in the past, whenever there have been moments of accountability that we’ve had to lead on, we are guided by three principles: follow the facts, apply the law and be guided by the United States Constitution,” the minority leader added.
House Democrats impeached Trump twice during his first term, but the Senate did not vote to convict him either time.
Clyburn on Sunday also spoke about Justice Clarence Thomas, who has been a crucial part of the Supreme Court’s conservative wing since he was first nominated by President George H.W. Bush in 1991.

During the confirmation process in 1991, Clyburn advocated for Thomas, telling a panel of senators at the time: “It’s a pleasure for me to be here today to present testimony in favor of my good friend Clarence Thomas. I have known Clarence for 10 years, and I consider him to be a personal and professional friend, in spite of the fact that he shares a conservative Republican philosophy.”
On Sunday, Clyburn said he was wrong to support Thomas three decades ago, telling “Meet the Press”: “I have made mistakes in my life, and that’s one that I made, and I will own up to that mistake.”
“I had no idea that Clarence Thomas would rebel the way he has against his own background and experiences,” the South Carolina congressman added.
Asked whether he supported a proposal by former Vice President Kamala Harris to expand the Supreme Court from nine justices to 13, Clyburn said, “I do.”

“I think that we are in a position now that calls for some significant actions taken by the Congress, and we ought to expand it,” he said. “Thirteen is a pretty good number; a baker’s dozen will be a good number to have on the court.”

title: Chicago mass shooting kills 1, injures 9 Saturday night
summary: Chicago police were trying to break up a gathering in the Washington Park neighborhood when gunfire rang out, with 10 victims struck.
story: Chicago police are investigating a mass shooting on the city’s South Side, with one person dead and at least nine others injured.
According to Chicago police, officers were attempting to disperse a large crowd in the 5400 block of South Cottage Grove Avenue just after 11:30 p.m. when gunfire rang out.
Police say at least 10 people were hit by gunfire in the shooting, which occurred in the city’s Washington Park neighborhood.
One of the victims, a 35-year-old man, was shot multiple times and was pronounced dead at the scene, according to the Cook County Medical Examiner’s Office.
Six victims who were shot were rushed to area hospitals and were listed in good condition, according to police.

Police are working to obtain information on three other victims, including a 37-year-old woman, a 23-year-old woman and a 35-year-old man. All three were taken to area hospitals, but their conditions are unknown at this time.
No Chicago police officers were hit by gunfire during the attack, according to authorities.
No suspects are in custody, and Area One detectives are investigating.

title: Sen. Ted Cruz calls for elections in Venezuela to proceed ‘rapidly’
summary: The Texas Republican also said the U.S. should arm protesters in Iran.
story: Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Sunday renewed his call for free and fair elections in Venezuela, just two days after the Trump administration announced that the U.S. would take over 65 billion barrels of oil from the South American nation.
“There need to be democratic, free elections in Venezuela,” Cruz told NBC News’ “Meet the Press,” adding later in the interview that elections should take place there “midway through next year.”
The acting Venezuelan president, Delcy Rodríguez, took over after U.S. forces captured then-President Nicolás Maduro in January and brought him to the U.S. to face drug-trafficking charges.

“Delcy Rodríguez was Nicolás Maduro’s vice president,” Cruz said Sunday. “Maduro was illegitimate. He was a Marxist. He had seized power contrary to the will of the voters, and from the beginning, I have been urging, and I believe the administration is working towards this, that there should be free and fair elections.”
The senator also praised the oil deal announced on Friday that will allow the U.S. to take control of 65 billion barrels of oil reserves from Venezuela.

“The oil deal as announced sounds like it could have a very positive impact on the United States and the United States economy, on American jobs, and a very positive impact on gas prices over the long term,” Cruz said, adding that he doesn’t think the U.S. needs to prioritize free and fair elections in Venezuela over the oil deal.

“I don’t think the timing matters as much as the one versus the other. I think the oil deal will move as rapidly forward as it can,” he said. “But I think free and fair elections need to proceed, and they need to proceed rapidly. I believe they should proceed no later than midway through next year.”
The Trump administration, the senator added, is “working rapidly to do that.”
Earlier this month, Cruz joined a bipartisan group of senators in introducing a resolution affirming the United States’ support for free and fair elections in Venezuela.

Cruz also spoke Sunday about the ongoing U.S. military conflict in Iran and called on the Trump administration to arm Iranian protesters to achieve a goal of “regime collapse” in the Middle Eastern nation.

“I would like to see the longer-term objective be regime collapse,” Cruz said, adding later: “What I’ve been urging is for President Trump and the Trump administration to arm the protesters, so that the people of Iran ... remove this regime from power. Not American boots on the ground, but the Iranian people.”
Days earlier, President Donald Trump posted an image on Truth Social declaring “mission accomplished” in Iran.
On Sunday, the senator said the “initial mission” in Iran — degrading the nation’s military capacity — was complete, but called for the removal of the ayatollah as a secondary objective.

Cruz also spoke about his presidential ambitions, which sparked headlines this week after he told MS NOW in an interview that the GOP has not automatically chosen Vice President JD Vance as President Donald Trump’s successor.
“There’ll be time to figure that out,” the senator told MS NOW, adding, “I’ll certainly be part of the discussion.”
Asked directly about whether he’s seriously considering a presidential campaign in 2028, Cruz said Sunday that he would make a decision after November’s midterm elections.

“The Book of Ecclesiastes tells us there’s a time for every season. This is not that season right now. This is the season of the midterms, and I’ll tell you, I’m spending my time on the road, campaigning for candidates all over the country,” the senator said.
“There will be a time for that conversation” about running for president, he said later in the interview.
Trump praised Cruz on Thursday when asked in the Oval Office about the senator potentially running for president in 2028.
“I would say that he’s very talented. He’s a very good friend of mine. I think he might do that, yeah. He’s a very — he’s a talented guy,” the president said.

Ten years ago, Trump and Cruz faced off in the Republican presidential primary as major foes. Trump went on to beat Cruz to win the GOP nomination and the presidency, but along the way delivered a stream of insults against Cruz, his father and his wife.

title: Dolly Parton’s niece shares emotional tribute after singer’s private funeral
summary: The country star’s funeral Friday was a private affair attended by family members, said her niece Lainey Parton.
story: Dolly Parton was laid to rest in a private funeral service attended by family on Friday, according to her niece.

Lainey Parton shared an emotional tribute post on Instagram on Saturday, writing: “This is a really hard post for me to make. I wanted to wait until after my granny was laid to rest yesterday before I tried to put any of this into words.”
Parton died Tuesday following a brief battle with cancer at age 80. Her social media pages said that at her request, a small private service would be held for immediate family.
Lainey remembered Parton as a loving and inspiring figure who “believed in me before I even knew how to believe in myself.”
“Because she couldn’t have kids of her own, she always made us feel like we were hers. She loved us that way, and I’ll forever be grateful for that,” she wrote.
Lainey shared a slew of photos from growing up with Parton, some from childhood and others taken onstage with the country star.
Lainey recalled singing with Parton on her 2024 “Smoky Mountain DNA” album, which included various Parton family members.

“I was a freshman in high school and SO nervous. But she had a way of making me feel like nothing bad could happen. She made me feel safe, confident, and like I belonged right there beside her,” Lainey recalled.
She said the music icon backed her decision to attend beauty school and helped her fund it.
“She didn’t just tell me to chase my dreams, she helped me get there,” she said.

“I’m so thankful I said yes to the opportunities and memories I got to share with her as my Aunt Dolly, including being in a movie with her. I’m so glad I have those moments to look back on now. I have things I can watch, hear, and hold onto when I miss her,” she continued.
While the family — and the world beyond — mourns Parton’s passing, Lainey said she’s holding on to the precious memories she shared with her “granny.”

“It still doesn’t feel real that she’s gone. I’m going to miss her voice, her laugh, her hugs, and just knowing she was there. I’m even going to miss those 4 AM calls, and I’d give anything to see her name pop up on my phone again,” she said.

“I feel incredibly lucky that I got to call her my granny. Thank you for always believing in me, loving me, and making me feel like I could do anything. I love you, Granny. Always,” she said, concluding her post.

The “Jolene” singer hailed from rural Tennessee, born into a large but tight-knit family. She was one of 12 children, and as her own family expanded, Parton maintained an incredibly close relationship with her siblings, nieces and nephews.

Her death sparked widespread mourning and emotional tributes from her fans, Hollywood and the music industry. The 11-time Grammy-winning singer-songwriter was more than just an artist. She was an icon who transcended genre and time, a philanthropist focused on children and poverty, and a businesswoman.
Parton was preceded in death by her husband of 59 years, Carl Thomas Dean, who died in 2025, and her parents, Avie Lee Caroline Owens and Robert Lee Parton Sr.

title: New Mexico man accused of fatally shooting cousin after argument over enchiladas
summary: Police say the men had been drinking and arguing before a fistfight broke out. A witness said the victim was walking away when Ervin Gutierrez pulled a gun and opened fire.
story: A New Mexico man is accused of fatally shooting his cousin after an evening of drinking escalated from an argument over enchiladas into a fistfight, according to an arrest warrant.
Ervin Joaquin Gutierrez, 22, is charged with an open count of murder in the Aug. 27 killing of Nathaniel Cavazos at an apartment complex in Albuquerque.

Gutierrez was arrested by Albuquerque police Friday evening and booked into the Metropolitan Detention Center shortly after midnight Saturday, according to jail records. He is being held on an open count of murder.

Albuquerque police responded to a shooting shortly before 11 p.m. and found Cavazos unresponsive in a pool of blood on the walkway between apartment buildings. He had been shot at least once and died from his injuries, according to the warrant affidavit.

A cousin of both men who told police he witnessed the shooting said Gutierrez had arrived earlier that afternoon to visit. The three later bought groceries, returned to the apartment and cooked green enchiladas while drinking alcohol, according to the affidavit.

The witness told authorities tension began when Gutierrez repeatedly claimed the chile on his enchiladas was hotter than the chile on Cavazos’ plate and challenged him to eat some. Cavazos responded that they had all eaten the same enchiladas, so the chile should be equally hot. The men continued arguing after the witness suggested they take his dog for a walk.

Eventually, Cavazos punched Gutierrez, and the two fought, according to the witness’ account. Cavazos struck Gutierrez enough to leave him bleeding before the fight ended and Cavazos began walking away, according to the affidavit.
Gutierrez then allegedly pulled out a handgun and confronted Cavazos, saying, “We’re family! We’re family! How could you do this to me?” the witness told investigators.
The witness said Cavazos was about 10 feet away and was not holding a weapon when Gutierrez fired three or four times, striking him in the back. Gutierrez then fled, according to the affidavit.
Police said the witness showed investigators a Snapchat message in which Gutierrez allegedly said Cavazos had threatened his life.
“Is he really dead?” Gutierrez allegedly wrote. “I did not want to kill him but i didn’t want him to kill me.”
Investigators said a handgun belonging to Cavazos was found at least 10 yards from his body.

title: College football player dies after collapsing on sideline moments after scoring touchdown
summary: William Jewell College in Missouri didn’t disclose the nature of junior running back MicahJo Barnett’s medical emergency.
story: A running back for William Jewell College in Missouri died Saturday after suffering a medical emergency during the first quarter of his team’s season opener, shortly after scoring a touchdown.
MicahJo Barnett, a junior business administration major at the Division II school, had a health crisis on the sideline following the score, according to a statement released by the college.
The home game against Fort Lewis College at Greene Stadium in Liberty, Missouri, was canceled after the incident.
Neither William Jewell athletics nor the NCAA, which also released a statement on Barnett’s death, disclosed the nature of his medical emergency.
Barnett was a Liberty native who played at Liberty North High School, where he helped lead the team to a state championship in 2023, according to records.

“Micah’s life was taken far too soon, leaving his family, friends, teammates, and community heartbroken,” read a message on a GoFundMe page set up for his family by one of his former youth coaches. The post described Barnett as “a talented and kind young man who was loved by so many.”

title: Rep. Jim Clyburn says impeaching Trump shouldn’t be Democrats’ priority if they win back the House
summary: The South Carolina representative also told “Meet the Press” that he regretted his support for Clarence Thomas during his Supreme Court confirmation hearings in 1991.
story: Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., said Sunday that Democrats should not prioritize impeaching President Donald Trump if they win control of the House in the upcoming midterm elections, but instead should focus on making life more affordable for Americans.

Clyburn told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that if Democrats take back the House, he feels confident that their first order of business would be making the country accessible and affordable for all citizens.

Pressed on whether he believes Democrats should rule out the prospect of impeaching Trump if they regain control of the House, the South Carolina lawmaker said, “I don’t rule it out, but I don’t rule it in.”

“I don’t think that should be our priority if we get into office,” he added. “Our priority ought to be making housing, education, energy, healthcare affordable and accessible for all of our citizens. Impeaching the president will not do that.”
His remarks come days after House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., was asked a similar question by CNN and said that he wasn’t ruling out impeaching Trump.

“We haven’t ruled anything in and we haven’t ruled anything out,” Jeffries told CNN, adding that he’s leaving those decisions up to the Democrats who would be in charge of the House Oversight and Judiciary committees if Democrats take back the House.

“As we’ve done in the past, whenever there have been moments of accountability that we’ve had to lead on, we are guided by three principles: follow the facts, apply the law and be guided by the United States Constitution,” the minority leader added.
House Democrats impeached Trump twice during his first term, but the Senate did not vote to convict him either time.
Clyburn on Sunday also spoke about Justice Clarence Thomas, who has been a crucial part of the Supreme Court’s conservative wing since he was first nominated by President George H.W. Bush in 1991.

During the confirmation process in 1991, Clyburn advocated for Thomas, telling a panel of senators at the time: “It’s a pleasure for me to be here today to present testimony in favor of my good friend Clarence Thomas. I have known Clarence for 10 years, and I consider him to be a personal and professional friend, in spite of the fact that he shares a conservative Republican philosophy.”
On Sunday, Clyburn said he was wrong to support Thomas three decades ago, telling “Meet the Press”: “I have made mistakes in my life, and that’s one that I made, and I will own up to that mistake.”
“I had no idea that Clarence Thomas would rebel the way he has against his own background and experiences,” the South Carolina congressman added.
Asked whether he supported a proposal by former Vice President Kamala Harris to expand the Supreme Court from nine justices to 13, Clyburn said, “I do.”

“I think that we are in a position now that calls for some significant actions taken by the Congress, and we ought to expand it,” he said. “Thirteen is a pretty good number; a baker’s dozen will be a good number to have on the court.”

title: Minnesota Supreme Court rejects Mike Lindell’s bid to recount GOP primary
summary: MyPillow founder Mike Lindell has long denied Donald Trump’s loss in the 2020 presidential election.
story: MyPillow founder Mike Lindell has long denied Donald Trump’s loss in the 2020 presidential election. Now, he’s refusing to accept his own election loss in the GOP primary for governor of Minnesota.
The Minnesota Supreme Court on Saturday rejected Lindell’s bid for a full recount of his Aug. 11 loss to state House Speaker Lisa Demuth after she won the Republican primary by 45,000 votes.

Chief Justice Natalie E. Hudson wrote in a six-page ruling that the Minnesota Secretary of State’s Office and its State Canvassing Board provided a recount plan that follows the law and are “not committing any wrongful act, omission, or error” as Lindell claimed.

Lindell told NBC News in a phone call Saturday evening that he plans to appeal the ruling to the U.S. Supreme Court. He said that his team is also requesting election data from all 87 counties through the Freedom of Information Act in order to pursue an independent investigation.
“I’m willing to pay even more money. I don’t care what it costs,” Lindell said.

Lindell previously pledged to pay an estimated $825,000 to cover a full hand recount and audit of the race but refused to pay the money on Monday, the state’s deadline, after finding out that the recount only included counting the ballots cast for either Lindell or Demuth.

Lindell sued the Minnesota secretary of state’s office and its State Canvassing Board Monday, claiming that they pulled a “bait-and-switch” on him by not counting the ballots for everyone in the seven-candidate Republican field.

The secretary of state’s office said in a statement Tuesday that it provided the contingent recount plan to Lindell after the State Canvassing Board approved it on Aug. 18, writing that “the plan follows state law and administrative rules on recount procedures and is consistent with previous recount plans.”

Hudson acknowledged in her ruling that Lindell argued “he is entitled to a full recount for both the Democratic and Republican primary races for governor ‘to ensure that there are no anomalies in the ballots, whether the votes cast are for the Democratic or Republican primaries,’ and that this recount must include ‘the recording of votes for every candidate.’”
“But Lindell’s focus on alleged anomalies confuses the purpose of a manual recount with an election contest,” Hudson wrote.

Hudson maintained that the recount plan approved by the canvassing board on Aug. 18 follows protocol, saying that during the recount, the ballots would first be sorted between those cast in the Democratic or the Republican primary and then the Republican ballots would be separated into three piles: one for Lindell, one for Demuth and one for all other candidates.

“In other words, after all votes are sorted and counted, Lindell would know whether he is the winner over Demuth,” Hudson wrote. “And all ballots, in all piles, would be counted and subject to challenge.”
Hudson’s ruling backs up Demuth’s victory in the GOP primary, reinforcing her spot in the general election against the Democratic nominee, Sen. Amy Klobuchar.

Lindell said Saturday he would not be satisfied with anything less than a full hand recount of all ballots cast in the Minnesota gubernatorial primary races, arguing that there were “anomalies” in the election data due to the use of electronic voting machines.
Before his own gubernatorial campaign, Lindell faced multiple lawsuits after he repeated debunked claims that the 2020 election was rigged by voting machines.
Lindell was found to have defamed a former employee of one company, Dominion Voting Systems, in June 2025. Lindell has denied the claim.

In another defamation case, Lindell has refused to pay $56,369 in sanctions to voting machine company Smartmatic USA Corp. Because he still has not paid what the court ordered, Lindell now owes even more than the original sanctions in court fees. He told NBC News this month that he still does not intend to pay either the fees or sanctions.

title: Dolly Parton Laid To Rest, Niece Shares In Emotional Post: ‘I Love You, Granny. Always’
summary: Iconic country star, philanthropist and actor Dolly Parton has been laid to rest, according to a social media post from her niece.
story: Iconic country star, philanthropist and actor Dolly Parton has been laid to rest, according to a social media post from her niece.

Lainey Parton shared an emotional tribute on Instagram to her “granny” after the private Aug. 28 ceremony. In the moving post, Lainey Parton described her famous aunt, who died on Aug. 25 at the age of 80, as a kind individual who treated her as her own child.

“This is a really hard post for me to make. I wanted to wait until after my granny was laid to rest yesterday before I tried to put any of this into words,” Lainey Parton wrote. “From the time I was little, my granny always had a way of making me feel like I was enough. She never made my dreams feel too big or made me feel like I couldn’t do something. She believed in me before I even knew how to believe in myself.”
Lainey Parton continued, saying that she “can’t think of” a single bad memory of her aunt.
“Because she couldn’t have kids of her own, she always made us feel like we were hers,” Lainey Parton wrote in the post. “She loved us that way, and I’ll forever be grateful for that.”

Dolly Parton died after “a brief battle with cancer” at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center in Nashville, Tennessee, according to a statement from her estate. In a video message posted on the singer’s Instagram, her nephew Bryan Seaver shared that Dolly Parton had requested a simple burial.

“Dolly was a farmer, just like her daddy. He farmed the soil, she farmed songs and happiness. Dolly called me and said she wants to rest in a beautiful bed of plush cotton because after a life wearing heavy rhinestones, she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest,” Seaver said in the video.
“Rest in peace, Aunt Dolly, Aunt Granny, Gigi. May God bless Dolly Parton, and may God bless you all,” he added. “She will always love you.”
In Lainey Parton’s social media post, the niece looked back on a warm memory she had of Dolly Parton, who had asked her to sing on the 2024 album “Smoky Mountain DNA: Family, Faith and Fables.”

“I was a freshman in high school and SO nervous. But she had a way of making me feel like nothing bad could happen,” Lainey Parton recounted. “She made me feel safe, confident, and like I belonged right there beside her.As I got older, she continued to believe in me.”
Lainey Parton also described how her aunt was supportive of her decision to go to beauty school.

“When I told her I wanted to go to beauty school, she never questioned why I wasn’t going to college. She told me she couldn’t see me doing anything else,” she wrote. “She financially supported me through school and helped me get my career started. She didn’t just tell me to chase my dreams, she helped me get there.”
Lainey Parton added that the loss still “doesn’t feel real,” but thanked those who have reached out in support of the family.

“I’m going to miss her voice, her laugh, her hugs, and just knowing she was there. I’m even going to miss those 4 AM calls, and I’d give anything to see her name pop up on my phone again,” she wrote. “I feel incredibly lucky that I got to call her my granny.”
Lainey Parton concluded with a message to her late aunt.
“Thank you for always believing in me, loving me, and making me feel like I could do anything.I love you, Granny. Always. 🤍” she wrote.

Dolly Parton’s death has sent shockwaves across the country. The beloved star was known for her philanthropy just as much as she was for her music. On Aug. 28, Tennessee Governor Bill Lee shared that he is partnering with the Nashville International Airport to rename the facility after Parton.

“At a place where Tennessee welcomes the world, it is fitting that Nashville International Airport would bear the name of our state’s favorite daughter and greet travelers with the enduring legacy of Dolly’s music, generosity, faith, and kindness,” Lee wrote in a press release.

title: Dolly Parton Becomes Most Streamed Artist Worldwide The Day After Her Death
summary: According to entertainment industry data and analytics company Luminate, audio streams of Parton’s music skyrocketed on Aug. 26, the day after the country star died of cancer at 80.
story: As the world grieves the passing of country icon Dolly Parton, many seem to be turning to her music to heal.

According to entertainment industry data and analytics company Luminate, audio streams of Parton’s music skyrocketed on Aug. 26, the day after the country star died of cancer at 80. That day she became the most streamed artist in the world with 79.7 million on-demand audio streams, the company’s data showed.
Parton’s music received an estimated 46.2 million streams in the U.S. alone. The most popular song was “Jolene” with four million streams, followed by “9 To 5” with 3.6 million streams.

“Islands In The Stream,” Parton’s hit with fellow country star Kenny Rogers, generated 2.9 million streams. And “I Will Always Love You,” which was famously covered by Whitney Houston, came in fourth with 2.8 million streams.
Luminate tracks music consumption data by looking at thousands of data sources, constructing a “musical entity database,” the company says.

Luminate’s data shows streams surged from Aug. 25, when the musician drew 37 million streams worldwide, already a 1,499% boom from the day before. In the U.S., the artist drew 27.7 million streams, a 2,350% increase from the day prior.
Parton passed after “a brief battle with cancer” according to her estate. She died at Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center with her loved ones by her side.

During her lifetime, Parton was no stranger to mainstream success and remains one of the best-selling country artists of all-time. Her music career, which began in the late 1950s, included 50 studio albums and over 100 million albums sold worldwide, according to Broadcast Music, Inc.
Parton’s music has long been critically acclaimed as well. The musician earned 55 Grammy nominations and 10 wins. In 2011, she was given the Recording Academy’s Lifetime Achievement Award.

title: Harry Styles Makes A Quip About Taylor Swift’s Wedding During MSG Show
summary: During a show at New York City’s Madison Square Garden on Aug. 29, singer Harry Styles appeared to make a quick quip about his ex Taylor Swift, who married NFL player Travis Kelce at the storied arena in July.
story: Oh my!

During a show at New York City’s Madison Square Garden on Aug. 29, singer Harry Styles appeared to make a quick quip about his ex Taylor Swift, who married NFL player Travis Kelce at the storied arena in July.
“From the Madison Square Garden, home of the world champion New York Knicks,” Styles says, shown in a video that captured the musician’s comment on stage. “They also do weddings!”
Fans, understandably, went wild as the video captures a roar from the audience shortly after Styles’ comment.

The show was part of Styles’ 30-concert residency at the Garden, entitled the “Together, Together” tour, which kicked off on Aug. 26. He is currently promoting his most recent album, “Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally,” which came out in March.

The venue just happens to be the site of the high-profile wedding between Swift and Kelce, which took place over the July 4 weekend and was attended by the likes of Tom Hanks and Jennifer Lopez. Their nuptials, according to a statement from the pair’s representatives sent to NBC News, were officiated by friend and comedian Adam Sandler. Instead of a traditional wedding party, Swift had her brother Austin Swift serve as the “man of honor,” while Kelce’s sibling Jason Kelce served as best man.

But more than a decade before the royal wedding, Swift and Styles, who fans lovingly referred to as “Haylor” at the time, were an item. They dated from late 2012 until early 2013. The two first met at the 2012 Kids Choice Awards. Rumors of their romance began to swirl in November 2012 when Swift was spotted, wearing a paper airplane necklace identical to that of Styles’. The next month, they were photographed walking around New York’s Central Park together.

The romance lasted just a few months with the pair breaking things off in January 2013. However, the two have seemingly stayed cordial over the years. And fans suspect that the relationship was the inspiration behind a few songs off of Swift’s album “1989,” including “Style” and “Is It Over Now?”

Styles is now reportedly engaged to actor Zoë Kravitz, though the couple has not publicly confirmed the news. During the opening night of Styles’ MSG residency, fans spotted Kravitz in the crowd. And the singer was filmed, giving her a thumbs up.

title: Tim McGraw Playfully Roasts His Own Onstage Fall
summary: Country star Tim McGraw took a tumble on stage Aug. 27 while performing his hit 1995 single “I Like It, I Love It” in Cincinnati, Ohio.
story: Oopsies!
Country star Tim McGraw took a little tumble on stage Aug. 27 while performing his hit 1995 single “I Like It, I Love It” in Cincinnati, Ohio. And the musician appeared to take it in stride.
In an Aug. 29 Instagram post, McGraw posted footage of the fall himself and poked fun at the mishap.
“Cincinnati, you started our weekend off on the right foot even if I couldn’t stay on mine 😂” McGraw wrote in the post’s caption. “We appreciate you coming out and singing along!”
McGraw, 59, is currently on the “Pawn Shop Guitar” Tour, named after his 2026 single of the same name. Cincinnati is one of more than 30 shows on the tour.

Video from the Aug. 27 set showed McGraw, working the crowd and grooving on stage to the hit song as fans belted out the lyrics. At one point, the heel of his boot appears to get stuck in a crevice, leading to the fall. Luckily, McGraw gets up quickly and continues the show, all smiles.
The highly-acclaimed country star is a longtime veteran of the stage, with a career that boasts more than 1700 concerts.

McGraw, who kicked off the shows in July, made his long-awaited return to touring after health issues forced him to cancel some of his 2024 “Standing Room Only” tour. The musician spent months, healing from a series of procedures which included multiple back surgeries and double knee replacements.
This latest tour comes before McGraw’s five-show residency at the Colosseum at Caesars Palace in Las Vegas that will be kicking off in the fall.

title: Taylor Swift Donates $50K To Mom Who Was Seriously Injured Saving Teens On Roadside
summary: Taylor Swift recently has made a significant donation to a Rhode Island mom of three who was seriously injured while helping a group of teens, NBC News has confirmed.
story: Taylor Swift recently has made a significant donation to a Rhode Island mom of three who was seriously injured while helping a group of teens, NBC News has confirmed.

The musician made a $50,000 contribution to a GoFundMe in support of Ashley Taunton, who on July 18 pulled over to help those in a car that had skid off the road during heavy rains, according to the fundraising page. While Taunton was assisting the teens in the car, another vehicle lost control on the road.
“In a split-second act of pure bravery, Ashley pushed the other person out of harm’s way, taking the brunt of the impact herself,” according to the GoFundMe page, which was verified by the platform.

Taunton — who sustained a number of injuries and, at one point, needed to be in a medically induced coma — wrote on Instagram Aug. 29 that she was moved by Swift’s generosity and that she was “overwhelmed with gratitude.”
“This is absolutely mind-blowing and so very humbling. @taylorswift you are a beautiful soul I wish I could hug you IRL,” Taunton wrote in her post.
Taunton’s husband Joe Taunton told local NBC affiliate WJAR that Ashley Taunton had been in the car with one of their daughters.

“When they were coming down 95 after exit four, another car in front of her hydroplanes went off into the woods,” Joe Taunton told the local NBC affiliate. “She pulled over... told my daughter to stay in the car and said, ‘Call Dad. I’m going to help the accident.’”
Joe Taunton told the outlet that his wife ran to help the teens. And while she was pulling one of them out of the vehicle, she was hit.
Ashley Taunton, who has been documenting her recovery on social media, shared that she spent 30 days in the hospital and underwent 3 surgeries.

“I can still remember the vehicle hurtling down the grass toward us. I remember pushing a teenager out of the way and praying I would get out of the way too, that didnt happen,” Ashley Taunton wrote in an Instagram post. “There was a huge smash, searing pain and the slow realization that I wasn’t going to get up from this one. Every moment since has been nothing short of miraculous!”

title: He Lived 10 Minutes From Where Dolly Parton Grew Up. She Helped Him Attend His Dream School
summary: Growing up in Gatlinburg, Tennessee, Dolly Parton was always a part of Gavin Harper’s life.
story: Growing up in Gatlinburg, Tennessee, Dolly Parton was always a part of Gavin Harper’s life.

The small mountain town is only 10 miles from Dollywood and about 16 from Locust Ridge, where Parton grew up. Earlier this year, Harper found out he had been chosen as the recipient of the 2026 Dolly Parton Scholarship, making his connection to the iconic late superstar even sweeter.

“Somebody should have told this kid in 12 years he’d be chasing dreams he doesn’t even know he has yet,” he wrote on Instagram in May, alongside a video sharing the news. “Thank you @dollyparton for helping make this kid’s dream come true.”
Parton died at the age 80 on Aug. 25, with fans and friends mourning the country icon, including Harper who posted a musical tribute to his “inspiration.”
In his video, he performs her 1987 song “Wildflowers” and notes that without Parton he “literally wouldn’t be where I am today.”

He recently started as a freshman at Belmont University in Nashville, telling NBC News that the $15,000 he got from the Dolly Parton Scholarship was the last bit he needed to attend his dream school where he’s studying songwriting.

“Dolly’s been a huge thing for me. And when I got in my freshman year (of high school), I fell in love with music completely,” Harper says, sharing he then knew he wanted to be a musician. “... And the best person I could look to was Dolly Parton because she grew up 10 minutes from my house.”

He shares how Parton was “everything” to his community. He says his brother was born at the Dolly Parton Birthing Unit at Covenant Health LeConte in Sevierville, Tennessee, and he attended elementary school “where all of her nieces and nephews went.” He was also part of Parton’s Imagination Library, which sends out free children’s books every month.
“I used to call her the Book Lady because she would always send books,” he says. “That’s just how I knew her as when I was young.”
When he was 14, he played at The Pines Downtown in Sevierville, “where Dolly played her first paid show when she was 10,” he says.
“I remember my mom made a huge deal of that, and it meant nothing to me at the time because I just didn’t understand it,” Harper recalls. “But now that means the world to me.”

This past year, he decided to apply to The Dolly Parton Scholarship, which is part of The Dollywood Foundation. The scholarship provides funds to students who “have a dream they wish to pursue and who can successfully communicate their plan and commitment to realize their dreams,” per the website.
Now enrolled in his first year of college and in the songwriting program, Harper is grateful for the opportunities Parton and the scholarship provided him.
“I just hope one day I can be as big an artist as Dolly,” he says. “And I hope that I can also give back to my community and be a good influence on the world.”

title: Justus Kelley Reacts to Being the 1st Miss USA to Be a Married Mom in Her 30s
summary: Justus Kelley made history as Miss USA winner who is a mom, wife and woman in her 30s. Here’s what to know.
story: Justus Kelley just made history as Miss USA 2026. She’s the first married woman, and the first woman in her 30s to win the pageant, Miss USA confirmed to TODAY.com.
The day after the Miss Virginia winner was crowned Miss USA 2026 on Aug. 27, Kelley tells TODAY.com what the moment of being crowned felt like.

“I feel like I left my heart on that stage, and I was so proud of what I had done this week, not just on stage, but each piece of how I decided to show up, bringing a message with me, doing everything with purpose and a mission in mind,” Kelley says.
“That, for me, is what I came to do, and so I really did feel like no matter what happens, I feel like I won. I just felt so much peace. I felt contentment.”
Until recent rule changes in 2023 and 2024, Miss USA prohibited women who were over the age of 28, or who were mothers, pregnant, married or divorced from entering the pageant.
As part of Miss USA’s 75th year celebration, Kelley was joined on stage by legacy queens.
“What we’re doing is only because of the shoulders that we’re standing on, the people that came before us,” Kelley says of meeting the legacy queens.

“I literally had to do my best to contain my excitement all week as I was meeting different former Miss USA’s, just in disbelief that I was meeting them in real life,” Kelley says. “These are women that I follow on social media and have followed throughout the years, and have looked up to them for so much of my life. So to now have these women be people that are welcoming me into a sisterhood just felt like a dream.”

Kelley is a foster parent. She and her husband, Tyler Kelley, are currently foster parents to a sibling set and have fostered previous children. Kelley is also the founder of Foster Footprints, a DMV-based foster support program.
She says she looks at her pageants, and the newest title, as a bigger way to raise awareness about the realities of foster care.
“I went to Miss USA, and I thought, how can I be intentional about my message and my purpose? Just being embedded in everything that I do,” she says.

“I’m very honest and transparent with people about how much I’ve learned since becoming a foster parent,” Kelley adds. “I had a little bit of an ignorance as to what kids would experience. I kind of assumed that every child in this situation must come from an awful situation or an awful parent. And my reality and what I’ve seen from the kiddos that have come into my home is they are coming oftentimes from families that deeply love them but are struggling, have fallen on hard times, are having housing crises and dealing with addiction.”

Kelley’s commitment to shedding light on the realities of the U.S. foster care system is evident in her Miss USA campaign. As she traveled to Miami, where this year’s competition was hosted, she carried trash bags. In an Instagram post, she explained why.

“The trash bags I carry reflect a reality far too many foster children know all too well. A trash bag should never be a child’s suitcase. Every foster child deserves to carry their belongings with dignity — and I need you to help me make that possible,” Kelley wrote in the caption.

The Arlington resident, who holds a master’s degree in public health administration, is also a senior philanthropic adviser for St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital in Arlington, according to her LinkedIn.
With pageant competitions as one of her many hustles, Kelley finds community. She tells TODAY.com what went into her decision to pursue the contests.

“I was a freshman or maybe sophomore in college at the time, just looking for community, looking for like-minded, strong women that wanted to empower and support each other, looking for those types of friendships,” she says. “I found that with pageant women, after doing my first one, I just loved it. I loved the experience and what I got out of it, being in a room full of women that inspire me. That is what keeps me coming back.”

Kelley says her family could not have been more supportive and proud throughout her pageant journey. She says they have been a part of this journey for several years, and that this dream of hers has become their dream.

“My husband keeps calling himself Mr. USA. I don’t know if that’s a thing. Every family member I talk to, they’re like, ‘I can’t believe I’m Miss USA’s aunt. I can’t believe I’m Miss USA’s sister,’ and I’m like, ‘What? Bro, I can’t believe I’m Miss USA.’ This is just  the coolest thing for all of us.”

title: When Is the ‘Love Island USA’ Season 8 Reunion?
summary: Find out everything you need to know about the “Love Island USA” Season 8 reunion, including when it will stream, so you don’t miss any of the drama.
story: It has been over a month since “Love Island USA” fans said goodbye to the Season 8 cast during the grand finale, and now it is time to catch up with the islanders to see if the romances and friendships have continued outside of the villa.

A few weeks ago, the cast, including winners Bryce Dettloff and Trinity Tatum, the “Core 4” and some divisive islanders came together to film a reunion hosted by Ariana Madix and Andy Cohen. Fans have been waiting to see if rumors about spats between contestants and more tension-filled moments are true. Soon, they’ll get their answers.

Ahead of the Season 8 reunion, Peacock released a teaser that showed Melanie Moreno and Sol Dean bickering, Kenzie Annis seemingly addressing a fallout with Melanie and KC Chandler still harboring resentment for the reactions to his Casa Amor behavior.
Plus, viewers will get to hear updates from Bryce and Trinity and the other finalists about everything that has happened since they re-entered the real world.
Find out everything you need to know about the Season 8 reunion so you don’t miss any of the drama.
When Is the ‘Love Island USA’ Season 8 Reunion?
The “Love Island USA” Season 8 reunion, led by host Ariana Madix and Bravo’s Andy Cohen, will be released on Monday, Aug. 31.
The reunion was taped in front of a live studio audience and it will feature all the OG islanders and bombshells fans couldn’t stop talking about all season long.
Where to Watch the ‘Love Island USA’ Season 8 Reunion
The reunion will stream on Peacock.
The streamer recently announced that “Love Island USA” will return for a ninth season next year with Madix as host.
Peacock previously confirmed that spinoff shows “Love Island: Beyond the Villa” and “Love Island Games” are both returning next year for their third seasons.
What Time Is the ‘Love Island USA’ Season 8 Reunion?
The reunion will be available on Peacock starting at 6 p.m. PT/ 9 p.m. ET.

title: KATSEYE Drops Out of Music Festival After Megan Skiendiel Is Injured
summary: KATSEYE has dropped out of Olivia Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields Festival in California after one of its members sprained an ankle in rehearsal this week.
story: KATSEYE has dropped out of Olivia Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields Festival in California after one of its members sprained an ankle in rehearsal this week.
The global girl group announced on its social medial channels Aug. 27 that it had to cancel its scheduled appearance at the festival on Aug. 29 in Irvine due to an injury to Megan Skiendiel.

“We’re so incredibly sorry to share that we are unable to perform at Daisy Chain Fields this Saturday,” the message reads. “Megan sprained her ankle yesterday during tour rehearsal and after being evaluated by doctors, she has been advised to stay off it and allow it to properly heal so we can be ready for our upcoming tour.”
The group said it broke their hearts “to disappoint anyone who made plans to be there.”
KATSEYE was expected to perform at 2:15 p.m. local time at the festival. An updated schedule shows Santigold performing in that time slot.

“We were especially excited for Daisy Chain Fields because it’s not just about music, but the greater mission of joy and community,” the group said in its statement. “We’re sending all our love to Olivia and to all of the incredible artists, non-profit organizations and volunteers who have given their time to make this day so special. It’s going to be such an amazing day, and we can’t wait to see everyone out on tour.”

Four members of the Grammy-nominated group —  Daniela Avanzini, Yoonchae Jeung, Lara Raj and Skiendiel — performed live on the TODAY Plaza Aug. 14 as part of the Citi Concert Series. Two other members of the group, Sophia Laforteza and Manon Bannerman, announced hiatuses from the band this year.
“As KATSEYE, it’s so important to us to always prioritize our well-being. We stand by Sophia and Manon through and through. We ride for them,” Raj said on TODAY.
Laforteza announced in early August that she was stepping away from the band to prioritize her “mental health and wellness.” Bannerman had previously announced her own hiatus in February.

The group’s sold-out world tour is scheduled to kick off on Sept. 1 in Dublin, Ireland, and will go across Europe before the North American leg kicks off on Oct. 13 in Miami. KATSEYE did not specify if Skiendiel’s injury would affect the upcoming tour dates.

title: ‘Finding Emily’ Director on Creating a Rom-Com That Satirizes Modern Dating, Cancel Culture
summary: “Finding Emily” director Alicia MacDonald tells TODAY.com how the film pokes fun at Gen Z and examines classic rom-com tropes with a modern lens.
story: Warning: This story contains spoilers for “Finding Emily”
“Finding Emily” takes the classic romantic-comedy format and rejuvenates it with a story that pokes fun at Gen Z and the current, chaotic state of modern dating.

The romantic comedy is set at the fictional Manchester City University in the lively English town. Owen, played by Spike Fearn, works as a sound engineer at the student union bar. One night, he bumps into, literally, a student named Emily (Sadie Soverall). Their adorable meet-cute turns into an evening of flirting about reusable straws and music. They have a connection and Owen gets her number before she hurries off. But the next day, Owen realizes that the number is missing a digit. Determined to find her, he teams up with an American psychology student also named Emily, played by Angourie Rice, to track her down. However, Rice’s Emily is secretly using the hopeless romantic as the subject of her case study about love being rooted in madness.

During his campus-wide search, Owen’s efforts go viral, with students there and abroad all weighing in on whether he has good intentions or is simply a persistent creep. Director Alicia MacDonald tells TODAY.com that the debate is what drew her to the film.

“I really loved that it had something to say,” she says about “Finding Emily,” which was released in U.K. cinemas in May and hits theaters in the U.S. Aug. 28. “It wasn’t just two people falling in love and there being chaos. It had something to say about what it is to be a romantic in this day and age and how complicated it is. That protest, cancel culture, gender, politics element was really interesting to me.”

MacDonald shares that she has always been a fan of satire and how it pairs so well with comedy. But, she notes that sometimes the two can clash and “alienate” audiences, which makes nailing the tone a challenge.
With “Finding Emily,” she accepted that challenge and used satire to examine tropes in past rom-coms.

“Those old rom-coms that had those grand gestures that we held up as iconic behavior — now today it’s, like, ‘Is that OK?’” she says about how some films have aged in our modern zeitgeist. “So l really liked that big question, as well as trying to balance in a coming-of-age element, which is something that I pulled out a lot more (from the script).”
“Finding Emily” leans into the university setting, introducing audiences to a variety of characters and their backgrounds, which influences how they view love.
“I hadn’t read anything that seemed to be interrogating how we love today,” she adds.

Below, she describes the perfect recipe for a rom-com and breaks down some of the film’s funniest and sweet moments, while also sharing how TikTok and more Gen Z fascinations were incorporated. Plus, she reveals her thoughts on fans telling her “rom-coms are so back” thanks to “Finding Emily.”
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

It was set there from the beginning. The writer (Rachel Hirons) is from Manchester. For me, it was such a big pull because so few films are set there, definitely not comedies. It’s such an amazing city. It has this incredible history of science and politics … They obviously have two wildly famous football teams, and the fashion is really cool. The music, of course, the music. And it all just radiates out of the city. It was such an exciting place to be. I lived there for six months and it felt so cool to put this city on screen which hadn’t been put on the screen before.

Oh, hugely involved! They’re all from my brain, one way or another. I’ve been making this playlist since I got the job. I felt a real responsibility to showcase Manchester bands, but not just the old, iconic ones. There were so many amazing new bands coming out of Manchester, and so much good music and different kinds of music. I was listening to so much and going to so many gigs. My music supervisor (Iain Cooke) was sending stuff, and Phil (Hignett), my editor, was making his own playlist. It was dictated by the story and what was happening, but I also really wanted a real rhythm and a pace to the film, so we’d feel kind of carried along with it.

That was Spike. That was just a little scene that I put in because I wanted Matt, his brother, to pick him up. I wanted it to be a small, nonverbal scene where he drives him back. Matt doesn’t have the words to cheer him up, but he knows that this song will. I spoke to Jack and Spike (about it). I think I’d been speaking about Tom Tom Club or something kind of ‘70s that would have felt like it was their mum’s favorite song or something that they’d all sung in the car together. Spike said, “Well, my mum’s favorite song is ‘Wordy Rappinghood’ by Tom Tom Club.” I played it on my phone. I’d heard it, but I didn’t really know it very well. I was like, “Yeah, this is amazing.” Because it’s really specific and unique, and that felt perfect for the story at that moment. There weren’t any backups. We just listened to that and went, “Yeah.” I spoke to the music supervisor and was, like, “What do you think?” He amazingly made it happen.

I hope I’ve just done it (laughs). I think it’s chemistry. I think these people don’t have to be perfect at all or overly likable, but they have to be honest and they have to be real. They’re both really complex and they have a lot going on. I think a lot of characters in rom-coms invariably have to learn vulnerability. I feel like a lot of characters are closed off, and they have to learn to be open. If you can find a way to do that, but have it feel human and real, (that’s it).

I think it’s this slight alchemy of soul in a film. I’m always ready to laugh, to cry, to be moved when I watch something. I think that comes from seeing people behave like human beings, just trying their best in this complicated world.

I have no idea what they mean when they say, “Rom-coms are back.” It’s being said all the time. I’m confused as to where they’ve been or what people are talking about. All I know is, I made a film that I really wanted to see. It’s (an) interesting thing about the genre because it’s got a sort of bad rep, or at least it has had a bad rep of recent. I guess that’s what people mean, right? Is that what people mean? That because of the straight-to-streamer ones, the cinematic ones are back? I don’t know.

We should ask one of these people who’s commenting, like, “What do you mean? Where have they been?” But I’m thrilled this one is in the cinema because I think they really belong there. I think all films (should have) a chance to be seen in the cinema because we all deserve to watch a story uninterrupted and really be immersed in it.
You’re the only person who’s noticed that really.

So all of those articles, I wrote all of them. I wrote them all in different journalist voices. Because I felt like if anyone ever pauses and wants to read, I really wanted them to be legit. Those social media montages ... it was quite a late decision in the edit. The reason why I ended up shooting the email sequence with all of the Emilies in Owen’s room is because I hate shooting phones because it’s so boring and I feel like we all hate seeing it. So, I’d initially not thought about a social media thing. But then you realize that you need to see the wider world. I was like, “How can we do it in a way that feels fun, that is informative and tells us what people are thinking, but that is also really, hopefully, funny and surprising?”

The reason why I ended up doing one is because we’d run out of actors and Emilies. So I just shot that with the editor ‘round the back of Abbey Road Studios. Then Phil, the editor, was like, “‘Come on, we should put you in the movie somewhere. Why don’t we make you there?’” I was like, “‘OK, in the sort of Hitchcock way.’” (The videos are) really important. I was very worried about getting them wrong and it feeling cringe. But so far people have said they’re OK.

It was pretty challenging because we wanted to do it in this oner and have them all appear as they do and do it all on camera. I didn’t want to do graphics on screen. Because I think that’s really claustrophobic. That feeling of having these people in your house, and that’s what we all feel when we’re on our laptops and stuff. It was complicated. We did a lot of takes. Everyone was super focused and dedicated to getting it right. But yeah, it was challenging.

The Canal Street scene with the 200 extras and drag queens and dancers and so much going on was also a challenge in a different way. But weirdly, yeah, I think maybe just getting that (Emily) sequence right (was difficult) because I also know we didn’t have a backup … It was stressful.

To be honest, I found it quite overwhelming. I’ve just been in my little flat in London, on my own, reading the comments. Because obviously you read all the comments. I thought I was going to be mature enough to not look at anything. I did hold off for a bit. It’s so amazing that people are responding so well, and it’s been so emotional. I found it a wild process because a lot of myself is in it, so it’s a very raw, vulnerable, overwhelming feeling to put something out into the world, which I hadn’t quite realized.

It’s been amazing, surreal, strange (and) existential somehow because it will live forever. When I was in London, I took myself to the cinema as a punter (the) second week that it was out. I thought I would get some kind of closure from watching it as I would normally a film. I went in and I sat down and I was next to this girl, and she was on her own. She had her sweets and her popcorn. She laughed and she gasped in all the right places. I obviously never said who I was. But it kind of felt like, “OK, this is OK. One person gets it.” It’s weird ... I thought I would feel better after seeing that, but it almost felt more surreal because I was like, “That’s my baby up there.”

Yeah, it was in the script. We developed it further as we got out. It’s a homage to The Verve’s “Bittersweet Symphony” video, and that was never the original plan. But I was speaking to Spike about what we could do, and he was like, “What about that? And get all the Emilies back?” And so we did. We tried to find somewhere that we could do it. It was obviously a more expensive way to do the end credits, but it was so fun. It felt like the right way to do it. We did (think) about whether you just leave it on them running away. But the music video is so fun. And that song, the proper produced version of (Owen’s) song, is so great. It was like, “Let’s give them a proper music video.”

title: The Opening Line of Leigh Bardugo’s Final ‘Ninth House’ Novel Sets Up This Major Change for the Series
summary: Leigh Bardugo shares Chapter 1 of “Dead Beat” with TODAY.com for “Cold Open” and unpacks the new perspective the novel is told from.
story: It is a truth universally acknowledged that a good story starts with a good first line. In TODAY’s “Cold Open,” authors tease their buzzy upcoming release by revealing and explaining its first line, paragraph or page.
Leigh Bardugo doesn’t enjoy writing finales.
“If you’ve read my books before, you know that I like complicated characters and complicated resolutions that aren’t always entirely happy,” she tells TODAY.com.

For “Dead Beat,” the third and final book in the trilogy that kicked off with 2019’s “Ninth House,” that means balancing a satisfying yet slightly hopeful ending with a desire to leave readers feeling “shaken.”

To wrap up the trilogy, protagonist Alex Stern must face increasing ranks of demons creeping in to prowl New Haven. Other obstacles in her way include: a corrupt Lethe Board, a deadly vampire and deep secrets in Yale’s societies, according to the novel’s synopsis.
TODAY.com has an exclusive first look at the book’s beginning, including the audiobook recording for Chapter 1, which opens with the following sentence:
When he had been a man only and not both man and monster, Darlington had understood his city and the bad bargains it had made.
That line establishes a key difference from “Dead Beat” compared to the rest of the trilogy: Darlington’s point of view.
“He has been a massive presence in the previous books, but we’ve only ever gotten a few chapters from his point of view,” she says. “He is much more present on the page in the third book.”

Darlington may be back in his human form, but he’s in a very different place, warring with specific impulses (Chapter 1 mentions a passing “pulse of desire” felt while looking at Alex), dealing with internal changes — and trying to combat both.
“Dead Beat” will feature a prologue, like the rest of the trilogy, told from Alex’s perspective at a key moment. The rest of the book moves backward “to figure out how we got there,” Bardugo says.

“The relationship between Alex and Darlington, the balance of power between them is very important to this third book. Alex’s relationship to all of her friends and allies — Alex is a character who has been fighting alone for a very long time. It is not natural for her to have to rely on other people,” she says.
Bardugo says ending the “Ninth House” trilogy brought “decision fatigue,” plenty of emotions and reflections on why she wrote the series, which marks her adult debut, in the first place.
“These are very strange books, and so I always feel like they somehow found people like me who would have loved to read these books,” Bardugo says. “This one’s for the weirdos, basically.”

It also marks the end of her “excavating” process reflecting on her own time at a student at Yale University. For her protagonist, Bardugo says that means leaving Alex in a place of “resolution” with her relationship to Yale and its institutions.
“These books are also wish fulfillment. They are the best things of this institution and also the worst,” Bardugo says.

Bardugo says “Dead Beat” will bring her “last tour for a long time,” but she’s excited to “go out with a bang.” Then, it’s back to writing. She says she’s working on an “ambitious horror project” with several other authors, set to be announced next year, and a graphic novel.
“And we also have some stuff brewing in the adaptation sphere, but I long ago learned not to count on anything,” she says.
Read the First Two Paragraphs of Leigh Bardugo’s ‘Dead Beat’

When he had been a man only and not both man and monster, Darlington had understood his city and the bad bargains it had made. He knew the changing shape of its harbor, the scars carved into its old neighborhoods by a deluge of federal cash that had seemed inexhaustible—as most floods do, until the drought arrives. He’d loved this tidy square named for a revolutionary general, its steepled church, its row of brownstones with their welcoming stoops. He had marveled at the strangeness of New Haven that could take a pocket neighborhood nestled against the noise and fumes of a highway and make it so desirable. The man he had been noted these things. He considered the branches of each cherry tree, black bones that would soften with pink in the spring.
The demon thought only of bodies. Human hearts tucked safely away in their houses.

title: 10 Reasons Dolly Parton Was A National Treasure
summary: Dolly Parton’s death has illuminated a life that was so much more than being a country music icon.
story: Dolly Parton’s death has illuminated a life that was so much more than being a country music icon.

The 10-time Grammy winner behind hits like “Jolene” and “9 to 5” died at 80 on Aug. 25. She left a legacy that has inspired artists across all musical genres and ages, as well as a reputation for philanthropy and kindness.
The way she lived her life made her beloved by millions and someone who will be studied by future generations.
Here are just 10 reasons why we consider her a true national treasure.

title: Tim Curry Named an Honorary Muppet, Joins Dolly Parton As 1 of Select Few With the Title
summary: The Muppets just paid tribute to legendary actor Tim Curry in the most fitting way.
story: The Muppets just paid tribute to legendary actor Tim Curry in the most fitting way.
The famous puppet troupe announced on their Instagram page Aug. 26 that Curry, who died this week at his Los Angeles home, has been posthumously bestowed the great standing of honorary Muppet.
In the post, the Muppets praised Curry, who starred as the iconic Long John Silver in 1996 film “Muppet Treasure Island,” describing the actor as “unparalleled.”

“Few humans have earned the title of honorary Muppet more than the legendary Tim Curry. As a performer he was unparalleled — witty, charming, unnerving, and deeply funny,” the post said. “We will always consider it one of our greatest treasures to have been part of Long John Silver’s crew. Thank you for everything, Tim.”

The actor, who died at 80 years old, joins Dolly Parton, who also passed this week on Aug. 25, as an honorary member of the beloved puppet troupe. Others, including comedians Robin Williams and Pee-Wee Herman are also part of the extremely selective group of human Muppets.

Curry, who’s known for his role in projects ranging from “Rocky Horror Picture Show” to “Home Alone 2,” has always been fond of the puppet crew. In his 2025 memoir “Vagabond,” he describes “Muppet Treasure Island” as “one of the best pictures I ever made” and “most apex of my big films from the 1990s.” The experience was truly life-changing for the actor.

“I cannot overstate how much I adored working with the Muppets,” Curry wrote in the book. “The extraordinary thing about them is that they are all characters in their own right, and you should treat them as such.”

The film, an adaptation of Robert Louis Stevenson’s classic, revolves around the adventures of a young orphan named Jim Hawkins who gets wrapped up in a swashbuckling adventure with Curry’s Long John Silver to find buried treasure.
The film, Curry wrote in his memoir, allowed him to tap into his feelings around the death of his own father, who passed away when the actor was 12 years old.

“There’s a whole improvised scene where Silver is trying to establish a rapport and relationship between himself and young Jim,” Curry wrote. “Having lost my father at a similar age, and for that to have been such a formative time for me, made my heart go out to Jim’s character in a very authentic way. I tried to imagine how I wished people had spoken to me when I was a boy.”
Curry added that there was a “real honesty” in the way in which he delivered his lines.

“Opening myself up in such a personal way wasn’t something I’d ever really experimented with before in film, and certainly not on the stage,” Curry wrote. “I had not planned on that bit; it just happened. In the end, I was very happy with it, though; it felt like a real risk in a very different kind of way, and I was proud of how I’d pulled it off.”
When filming wrapped, Curry wrote, he found himself missing the project.
“I was genuinely saddened to return to dealing with humans again,” the actor said in the memoir.

The Muppets also have a special place in his heart for another reason. While Curry was famously committed to keeping his love life private, he was openly crazy about one particular gal: Miss Piggy. In the book, Curry  describes the fabulous ham as “always funny, and never boring.”

“Although I did say at the outset that I wouldn’t speak about any of my romantic relationships, I will say that Miss Piggy and I had quite a good time together, both on set and in our trailers,” he joked. “Fortunately, our dalliances never led to any tension with Kermit—I was clever about it.”

title: Kathryn Stockett’s Friends Told Her to ‘Find a New Profession’ After ‘The Help.’ Instead She Wrote Another Bestseller
summary: Kathryn Stockett spoke to Jenna Bush Hager about the road to “The Calamity Club,” a bestselling novel also set in Mississippi.
story: Seventeen years after “The Help,” Kathryn Stockett is back with “The Calamity Club,” a bestselling novel also set in Mississippi.
On the Aug. 27 episode of “Open Book with Jenna,” Stockett spoke about her long journey to the followup — so long, in fact, that her friends advised her to “find a new profession.”

“The Help” was a hit on a scale that authors dream about. After receiving over 60 rejections from literary agents, Stockett finally got her break, and that Mississippi-set story led to a publishing phenomenon. Published in 2009, the book sold millions of copies and inspired an Oscar-nominated movie.

But it also attracted tremendous controversy. Stockett’s first novel, in part, followed Black domestic workers at a house in Mississippi, and she said she modeled their voices on the women she knew growing up in her family’s employ.
The book and movie sparked a dialogue about race, representation and who should tell whose stories, with star Viola Davis ultimately saying she regretted being part of the film.
After publishing her controversial juggernaut, Stockett retreated from the public eye and started working on her next book. And worked. And worked.
Stockett told Jenna she was committed to writing “a really short book that didn’t draw the same criticisms that ‘The Help’ did.”
“I was like, ‘I’m not going to stir the pot with this one,’” she said.
But the book wasn’t coming along, she said, because she “wasn’t telling the truth” in her writing.

As the time wore on, Stockett said the people in her life became concerned she was wasting her time. “People started looking at me. My friends started to say, ‘Kitty, I think you need to move on.
